en: *The Authentic Explanation of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
Fascicle One Annotated by the Layman Shengxian, Gong Jicai;
Verified by the Layman Lianfang, Hu Zhengzhi.
Section One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly. (Dharma refers here to the Mahāyāna Dharma. Assembly refers to the Buddha’s gathering with his disciples at the Jeta Grove.
"Cause" (yin) means the beginning; "condition" (you) means practice. Practice must have a beginning. This Dharma assembly constitutes the causes and conditions for the composition of this sutra.)
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was [staying]... until having put away his robe and bowl and washed his feet, he spread out a seat and sat down.
[Note: "Thus" (*evam*) refers to the Dharma spoken in this sutra. "I" (*aham*) is the self-designation of the compiler of the sutra;
it is Ānanda. He states that he personally heard this Dharma from the Buddha. "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers to the master and disciple...

Encounter. At the time of expounding this Prajñā, "Buddha" means awakening. Because he has awakened himself and awakened others, and because his practice of awakening is perfected, he is named Buddha.
This refers to Śākyamuni, who is the sole Teacher. Śrāvastī:
the Sanskrit name is Śrāvastī, which here means "Hearing of Things. It is the kingdom of King Prasenajit. Jeta’s Grove: [the grove] of King Jeta.
The son’s name was Jeta, which in this [language] means "Victory in Battle. He was so named because his birth coincided with a victory in battle.
As for the tree, it was donated by Jeta. Regarding the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden: the king’s minister was named Sudatta (alternatively, *Suta*).
He constantly resided in this garden, providing relief to the orphaned and the solitary. Sudatta was originally a follower of non-Buddhist paths; however, while staying in Rājagṛha...
The Elder’s family heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, and a heart of reverence arose within them.
Desiring to secure an excellent site to invite the Buddha to reside, they thought of the Prince’s garden, which was eighty *krośas* in extent, spacious, pure, and fit to be a ground for merit.
They went to inform the Prince, who said in jest, "If you spread gold to fill the entire garden, I shall grant it to you. Sudatta acted accordingly.
He said: "The Prince did not covet gold either; he took the gold to jointly establish a vihāra and invited the Buddha to preach the Dharma.
'Bhikṣu' is a Sanskrit term; in the language of the Huá (Chinese), it means 'one who begs.

This refers to begging for the Dharma from the Buddha above, in order to clarify one's own true nature, and begging for food from others below, in order to plant seeds of merit for worldly people—these are the monks of today. As for 'Mahābhikṣu,' it is..."
Those who have attained the profound depths of the Way are revered by both devas and humans; this is not because they possess only minor virtues.
They are extensively versed in both internal and external scriptures; this is not because their understanding is limited.

Indeed, when the Buddha was about to expound the supreme, wondrous principle of true emptiness, only those who had attained the profound depths of the Way were capable of inquiring and gaining realization. Thus, all one thousand two hundred and fifty people...
The disciples whom the Buddha had converted and taught, who constantly followed him to listen to the Dharma, were all present.
At that time—meaning at that moment—the World-Honored One, who is revered by all people in the world, was at the time for eating, the time for begging for alms, not yet the time for receiving food;
the hour for begging for alms was then past, while the hour for receiving food was at noon. He put on his robes, specifically donning the saṃghāṭī. That is to say:
The great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) consisting of twenty-five strips is fashioned like a water paddy field;
because seeing it generates merit, the Buddha decreed that when entering royal cities or villages, one should wear this robe—just as the *kaṣāya* is worn today.

As for the alms bowl, he held the bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings (which was the bowl of the past Buddha Vipaśyin; after his parinirvāṇa, it was enshrined in the palace of the Dragon King. When Śākyamuni attained enlightenment, the Dragon King brought it out upon the waters of the sea, and the Four Heavenly [Kings...])

The king took it to offer to the Buddha; this is the bowl of deep blue lapis lazuli, which he used when going on almsround. He practiced sequential begging, wandering for alms with equanimity, making no distinction between the poor and the rich or the noble and the lowly.
"The original location" refers to the Jeta Grove. Regarding the phrase "having finished the meal," the character *fàn* (飯) should be understood here as the character *cān* (餐).
This refers to the time of receiving food; "completed" means finished. "Washing the feet": because people in the Western Regions (India) walk barefoot, they wash away dust and grime with water.
"Having done so" means it is finished. "Spread out" means to lay out. He arranges the high seats and sits upon them; this is what is known today as sitting in meditation (*zhìjìng*).
He does this because he is about to preach the Dharma.
[Commentary] Ānanda recorded and said: "What is spoken in this sutra was indeed heard by me personally from the Buddha.

When the Buddha preached this sutra, he was in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus who had attained the Way, as well as a following of one thousand two hundred and fifty people who were listening to the Dharma."

At that time, when the sun was at the hour of Si (the fourth watch), the proper time for begging for food, the World-Honored One donned his saṃghāṭī robe, took up his deep-blue lapis lazuli bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī from the park outside the walls.

He proceeded on his alms-round in regular order, not bypassing the poor to follow the wealthy, nor abandoning the lowly to follow the noble; with great compassion, he was impartial and without distinction.
There was a choice. Having finished begging for alms, he returned to the grove. At midday, he received his meal;
when the meal was finished, he was about to enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Thereupon, he put away his robes and bowl so that his mind would be free from attachments.
He washed his feet to purify his body, then spread out his seat and sat down. Thus, the causes and conditions for preaching the Dharma arose.

Section Two: The Inquiry of Subhūti (This section is divided into two parts. Subhūti is an alternative name for Śāriputra. At the time when the World-Honored One was seated cross-legged, it was the occasion for his principal disciples to request instruction;
therefore, he rose with reverence and posed his questions).
At that time, the Elder Subhūti was among the great assembly... [down to] "...how should one subdue the mind? [Note]:
"At that time" refers to the time when Subhūti raised his question. Among the assembly of disciples, those who were preeminent in virtue and advanced in years were called "Elders.
Subhūti is also named Shanxian (Sudatta) and is further referred to as Kongsheng (Śūnyatā-ja). As for the Venerable One's initial...

At the time of his birth, his house was completely empty. A physiognomist divined his future and declared it to be exclusively auspicious and fortunate; thus he was named Śākyamuni (Śākyasiṃha), which means "Exclusively Auspicious.

Regarding *piānbàn* (偏半): it means to baring one shoulder. As for the garment he wore, it left his right shoulder partially exposed. In the Eastern Land (China), baring the shoulder is considered an act of negligence;
in the Western Land (India), baring the shoulder is considered an act of reverence. This signifies his request for the Dharma of Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment, which he bears upon his own person.
[He] places his right knee on the ground. The right represents the Right Path; the left represents the Deviant Path.

This also symbolizes requesting the True Dharma, taking refuge in reality, and receiving it with humble prostration. He joins his palms in reverence. In the Eastern Land [of China], joining the hands in front of the chest is considered respectful.
In the Western regions, joining the palms is the mark of reverence. With both hands joined together, one maintains a solemn and respectful posture with the body unwavering;
the mind is single-pointedly focused, and the expression of sincere devotion remains constant. "I ask" (*pṛcchāmi*) means to inquire. Subhūti addressed his inquiry to the Buddha;
these aforementioned seven phrases are all the compiler’s narrative introduction. "Rare indeed" (*āścaryam*) means difficult to encounter even throughout vast eons.

"Encounter. A single Buddha in a thousand worlds is a rarity in the world. Regarding the epithets used to praise the Buddha: "Tathāgata" is a general title for a Buddha, analogous to the Chinese term "sage" (shèng rén).
"Thus" (tathā) means not being born; "come" (āgata) means not perishing. This refers to the essence and function of true nature.

This is for the purpose of establishing a name. *Hù* (護) means to protect; *ài-hù* (愛護) means to cherish and protect. *Niàn* (念) means to keep in mind; *cún-niàn* (存念) means to maintain mindfulness. *Fù* (付) means to entrust; *fù-shòu* (付授) means to hand over.

*Zhǔ* (囑) means to exhort; *zhǔ-gào* (囑告) means to instruct and inform. *Bōsà* (菩薩) is originally called *pútí-sàtuó* (菩提薩埵). Its characters were abbreviated for the sake of ease in recitation, hence it is called *bōsà*.

*Pútí* (菩提) in the language of China means "awakening" (*bodhi*). *Sàtuó* (薩埵) in the language of China means "sentient being" (*sattva*). One who awakens sentient beings is so called because sentient beings generally possess many worldly desires.

Yet they are unable to awaken. Only the Bodhisattvas, dwelling among sentient beings, are able to awaken by themselves without being defiled, and furthermore, they are able to awaken sentient beings and guide them.
"Bodhisattva" (諸菩薩) refers to those who study under the Tathāgata. *A* means "no"; *nuttara* means "supreme"; *samyak* means "correct."

"Vipula" means equality; "bodhi" means awakening, specifically referring to the Unsurpassed, Perfect, Equal, and Right Awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is a designation for the True Mind.
This mind encompasses the great void; since nothing can surpass it, it is called "unsurpassed.
Furthermore, from the Buddhas above down to the most minute insects below, this mind’s true nature is equal; therefore, it is called "perfectly equal. Its awakening is perfect and...

Its brilliance shines universally; being without partiality or deficiency, it is called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*). "How indeed? (*kathaṃ nu*) is a phrase used to request the Buddha to speak.
"Should" (*yuan*) means "it ought to be. "Abiding" (*zhu*) means "to dwell. "Subduing" (*jiangfu*) refers to the act of restraining and controlling.
[Commentary]: Subhūti, from within the great assembly, rose from his own seat, adjusted his dignified demeanor, and bared his right shoulder to show that he did not dare turn his back on the Teacher;
he knelt with his right knee to show that he did not dare deviate to the left from the Path;
he joined his palms to show his taking refuge, and manifested his reverence to show his solemnity. And...
He addressed the Buddha to offer his inquiry, first offering praise, saying: "Among all that is small in the world, our World-Honored One is supreme.

He further said: "The Tathāgata has given rise to a heart of compassion, skillfully protecting and cherishing the assembly of bodhisattvas within this gathering, causing them to receive it with faith, and skillfully entrusting and consigning these Buddha-dharmas to them."
He caused the assembly of bodhisattvas within this gathering to practice and uphold it. He then asked again:

“World-Honored One, if there are good sons or good daughters who, at the beginning of their study of the Way, give rise to this mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how should they abide so as to remain steadfast and never fall back, even unto the point of delusion?”
"When a thought arises, by what path should one subdue it so that it does not delude my true mind?
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti... [up to] "...Yes indeed, World-Honored One; I wish to hear it with joy."
[Note] "Excellent, excellent" (*sādhu sādhu*) is a term of praise. "Carefully examine" (*samanvāhara*) means to listen attentively. "You should" (*yoniśaḥ*) refers to these two phrases.
One interpretation states that the following two sections constitute the exposition; this [current section] merely serves as an introduction to prompt careful listening.
This view is overly abstract, recognizing only that it directs one toward what follows. Others take it to refer back to the preceding text.
"This very [mind] can abide; this very [mind] can subdue. This refers directly to the arousal of the bodhicitta as a term of certification (*anujñā*).
This is because it is viewed too concretely; one merely knows how it follows from what precedes it.

I venture to say that these two characters, "thus" (*evam*), carry reality within their emptiness, following from the preceding arousal of the bodhicitta, while maintaining emptiness within their reality, reflecting downward upon...

The phrase "going forth to bestow upon those to be saved" (du-sheng boshi qu) constitutes the thematic thread of the discourse. Generally, it is easy for people to understand how the illumination below gives rise to [the realization above];
however, the state at the summit is ineffable. To reach the ultimate limit would obstruct the subsequent text; thus, one must simply decline.
Nevertheless, this accords with what he has already said regarding listening attentively—some might compare it to the "One Thread" (yige) of Master Zeng in the Confucian scriptures.
This refers to perceiving [the object] too deeply. It means that the mind aspires to it, the mind of delight finds pleasure in it, and the mind of desire thinks of obtaining it;
this is a detailed explanation of how the mind aspires to, delights in, and thinks of obtaining hearing, abiding, and subduing.

[Commentary: Because Subhūti’s inquiry was perfectly in accord with the Buddha’s own mind, the Buddha praised him by saying repeatedly, "Excellent! Excellent! He then followed Subhūti’s words and said:
"Since you have been well-guarded and well-entrusted by the Tathāgata, you have skillfully brought forth my unspoken words. You should listen with careful attention. I— [text continues]
I shall now explain for you this path of abiding in subjugation.

Although the bodhicitta—the mind of enlightenment—is inherently present within all people, they are nevertheless submerged in worldly desires, and those who attack and seize it increase day by day. It is most difficult to arouse;
yet, once a virtuous man or woman has aroused this mind, they should abide in it and subjugate their deluded mind in this manner.
Subhūti, having spoken thus, addressed the World-Honored One once more, saying, "I, your disciple, wish to hear his teaching.

Section Three: The True Principle of the Mahāyāna. (Mahāyāna means that which is not the Hīnayāna. Within the Buddha-dharma, there are both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, much as Confucianism has the Great Learning and the Elementary Learning.

Bodhisattvas employ this Mahāyāna Dharma to transform and guide sentient beings; it is like a vehicle for carrying things, whose capacity for transport is exceedingly great. *Zong* (principle) refers to what the mind takes as its primary focus. *Zheng* (correct) means correct, as opposed to deviant.)
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattvas [up to] those who perceive the mark of a sentient being or the mark of a life-span are not bodhisattvas.
[Note: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas" refers to the assembly present at the gathering. *Mahā* means "great.
A great awakened being (*mahāsattva*) is one capable of delivering others. "Thus" points to what is taught in the following text. "Sentient beings" (*sattva*).
This refers to all classes of living beings, from the various heavens above down to humans and animals below. Although sentient beings are numerous, they can be categorized into nine types:
namely, those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those with form and those without form; and those with perception and those without perception.
It is neither with perception nor without perception. "I" is a term used in relation to the assembly;
it is a phrase employed by a Bodhisattva who vows to save sentient beings on their behalf, not a self-designation of the Buddha. "All" means to exhaustively complete. "To cause" means to command.
"To enter" means to enter therein, leaving nothing remaining; outside of this, there is nothing further. This is the Great Nirvana, for all practitioners.
"Refuge" refers to the fundamentally pure state of the mind of true emptiness. "Extinction" means to extinguish all ignorance and afflictions.
"Deliverance" means to cross over and liberate oneself from the ocean of suffering of birth and death. The Bodhisattva’s mind is impartial;
they universally vow that all sentient beings shall together enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder. "Measure" refers to a limited quantity or number.
"Number" refers to the limits of the boundaries. "Immeasurable," "innumerable," and "boundless" are the ultimate terms for expressing great quantity.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refer to physical traces; to cling to these traces so that the mind is not empty, becoming stagnant and failing to transform—this is called "existence.

As for the "characteristic of self" (ātman), it is to identify the four elements as one's own possession, thereby forming the characteristic of self. The characteristic of "person" (pudgala) is relative to the self.
It is said: "The mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*) refers to all those who have come into existence. The 'mark of a life-span' (*jīvitāśin-nimitta*) signifies longevity and non-extinction;
it carries the meaning of enduring duration.
[Commentary] The Buddha told Subhūti: "The various great Bodhisattvas, wishing to subdue their deluded minds, cause them to..."
Regarding those who dwell securely in the true mind: by what path is this fruit attained? An ordinary person’s single body consists entirely of the five aggregates and six consciousnesses;
because these obscure my true nature, when I interact with all sentient beings, it is difficult to subdue my deluded mind when it is stirred.
Why is this so? Because the nature is easily light, prone to soaring, and restless. Or...
Those who are called "egg-born" (aṇḍaja) due to their physical shells are those whose consciousness constantly transmigrates and whose habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are deep and heavy.
Those who are called "womb-born" (jarāyuja) due to their fetal membranes are those whose minds follow false views, sinking into delusion without awakening.

Those who are called "moisture-born" (saṃsvedaja) due to their attraction to dampness are sentient beings who pursue shadows and appearances, drifting through transformations and giving rise to illusions. Or they follow through miraculous transformation (nirmāṇa).
Regarding those termed "born by transformation" (*upapāduka*): those who grasp at the characteristics of cultivation as causes and cling to the view of form are called "possessing form" (*rūpin*).

Those who remain silent and guard emptiness while stubbornly clinging to the view of formlessness are called "formless" (*arūpin*). Those who are hindered by various hearsay and views, and whose mindfulness is bound up in defiled attachment, are called "possessing perception" (*saṃjñin*).
Those who have severed thought so that it does not arise, resulting in a state of empty guarding of silence, are called... [unperceiving].

Those who perceive neither thought nor non-thought, yet give rise to views of arising and ceasing, and whose faculties fall between the two extremes of existence and non-existence, are called "neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving.
All these nine classes of sentient beings are deluded regarding the Truth and pursue the false; their dispositions differ, and they arise from conditions based upon their natures.
Their deluded minds establish their states, and they take birth according to their kind—whether as devas, humans, or animals—even as vast as empty space.
Gods, the demons of the *yāma*, and other spirits are submerged in the worldly realms, transmigrating through birth and death.
From the lowest realm of desire up to the various heavens, they cycle through the six paths of existence, making it difficult for them to enter *nirvāṇa*.

Because they respond to delusion with further delusion, they stir my deluded mind, giving rise to discriminatory views that are difficult to subdue. Now, I shall immediately give rise to the mind of equal and perfect enlightenment; then—
The original minds of sentient beings are no different from my own mind. I shall cause all to dissolve their afflictions and transform their attachments;

they shall awaken from delusion and realize the truth, shatter their ignorant views, extinguish the fire of ignorance, and enter the wondrous realm of pure, unconditioned nirvana, thereby attaining parinirvāṇa. Such parinirvāṇa is immeasurable and beyond calculation.
It is boundless. How could there truly be "sentient beings" among all sentient beings whom one might cause to enter nirvana and deliver?
It is simply that sentient beings originally possess this bodhicitta; it is only because they are deluded and do not awaken that they give rise to various kinds of false appearances.
Now, by causing their minds to suddenly and brilliantly open up in a single day, their fundamental natures are entirely transformed. Instantly...
To see that the fundamental nature is empty and quiescent is for one’s own nature to deliver itself. Originally, there is no such thing as a sentient being;
how then could one bring them to extinction? Indeed, there is truly no sentient being who attains extinction. Why is this so?
It is because the fundamental nature is originally empty, devoid of the traces of self, person, sentient being, or life-span. This is the Unsurpassed.
Only one who possesses the bodhicitta is truly a Mahāsattva.

If one possesses these four characteristics, then regarding all sentient beings previously mentioned, one will falsely engage in discrimination, give rise to wrong views in the mind, and produce various afflictions.
How then could one cause them all to attain extinction and reach nirvana? Such a person is certainly not one who occupies the stage of a Bodhisattva.

Section Four: On Sublime Practice Without Abiding (divided into two parts. "Sublime practice" refers to the refined and wondrous conduct cultivated toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. "Without abiding" means not being bound by or attached to such refined and wondrous conduct;
it is fundamentally free from dwelling in attachment).
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva regarding dharmas... does not dwell [on them] while practicing giving of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or dharmas.
[Note: "Furthermore" (*fù*) means again; "next" (*cì*) means a second time. This is the narrator’s phrase, stating that he spoke again to Subhūti.
According to the *Zōngzhù* (Commentary on the Essential), "next" (*cì*) refers to the seating order. Subhūti had previously risen from his seat and knelt to inquire.
Upon reaching this point, the messenger returned to his seat and informed him. Furthermore, the two characters "Fo" (Buddha) are the words of the Buddha;

"Subhūti" is the name by which he is called and addressed. These may also be recorded as supplementary references. Regarding the phrase "the Dharma of dharmas," it generally refers to the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the statement "the phenomena of contact and mental objects": all that belongs to the mental faculty’s discrimination and conceptualization is pervasive distribution (*prabhāvanā*) and relinquishment (*tyāga*).
Form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects constitute the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind constitute the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

The eye engages with form; the ear engages with sound; the nose engages with odor; the tongue engages with taste; the body engages with touch; and the mind engages with mental objects—these constitute the six [sense-bases].
"Entering. As for "contact," it refers to that which comes and impinges upon the body. That which is like being full, warm, and at ease is pleasant contact (*sukha-sparśa*).

That which is characterized by toil, pain, hunger, and cold is painful contact (*duḥkha-sparśa*). As for "dharmas," these are what the mind raises up—namely, the categories of deliberation and discrimination regarding right and wrong.
Those that accord with principle and truth are wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*); those that stir up emotional desires are unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*). As for "abiding":
This means abiding within the sense faculties and their objects while remaining attached and untransformed. One does not abide in giving;
for example, when giving form to others, one does not harbor a mind that clings to the act of giving form. The same applies to sounds, fragrances, and so forth.
[Commentary] The Buddha spoke again to Subhūti: "A bodhisattva, regarding all dharmas practiced, should practice giving without any attachment.
To say that one gives with form is to be attached to form; the same applies to sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
This is because ordinary people, out of greedy attachment, plant merit through giving; this constitutes dwelling in signs."
Ordinary people are attached to objects when practicing giving; however, the Bodhisattva practices giving having realized that all things are fundamentally empty.

Not dwelling on form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena, his giving is free from obstruction. This is how one ought to practice non-attachment; it is precisely thus that the Bodhisattva practices giving. This is the proper principle.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give alms in this manner... [up to] ...a bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed. [Note]:
"Marks" (lakṣaṇa) refer to the marks of the six sense organs and the six sense objects. "Merit" (puṇya) refers to the merit within the nature.
The Buddha feared that people might doubt that by not abiding in marks one would fall into a state of inert emptiness; therefore, he spoke of "merit" to awaken them. Merit.
Immeasurable. The karmic reward is likewise immeasurable. When the Buddha speaks only of "merit," he means that the bodhisattva merely cultivates merit without looking for its reward.
"Inconceivable" means it is vast; one cannot use the mind to calculate its magnitude or quantity. "What do you think?
asks him to consider what principle you would apply in your own mind. [The four intermediate directions.]

The four corners refer to such directions as southeast, northwest, and so forth. East, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, and above and below are collectively termed the ten directions (*daśadig*).
As for "empty space" (*ākāśa*), within the great void there is not even the slightest obstruction or impediment.
It is vast, empty, and luminous, beyond the capacity of thought or mind to measure.

Because the Buddha’s merit and virtue are inconceivable, he employs the emptiness of the ten directions as a metaphor. How could emptiness itself be conceived? Therefore, Subhūti, they all reply, "No.
That he addresses him as "World-Honored One" at the conclusion of his speech is an expression of the utmost reverence. [The text] encompasses emptiness with...
"The ten directions" refers to the entire substance of empty space; it is not a mere void of insentient matter. "As such" refers back to the aforementioned empty space.
[Commentary] The Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying: "A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner, without dwelling [on anything]."

Regarding characteristics: Why is this? If a bodhisattva practicing the path does not become attached to the sense bases and objects—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—and practices giving with a mind of joyful relinquishment that is empty, their merit will be perfected, equal in measure to space.
How could it ever be possible for the human mind to fathom, gauge, or measure it? He asked again: Subhūti...
"Bodhi, what do you think? Can the space of the eastern direction be measured by the mind?
Subhūti replied, 'It cannot be measured. He further asked regarding the spaces of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below:
can they be measured? Subhūti likewise replied, 'They cannot be measured.'"
Indeed, there is nothing greater than empty space; it cannot be measured by human means.
Furthermore, the Buddha has clearly stated that the merit of giving without abiding in signs is likewise as inconceivable as empty space.
Thereupon, the Buddha called out and addressed them: "Those bodhisattvas who study the Way need not seek it elsewhere."
It should descend below the state of abiding. You must simply rely on my teaching to you: the dharma of giving without the mark of abiding.
Then, let it rest right here within the sphere of preservation and nourishment, as profound and still as the empty space of the ten directions;
it is permissible to abide by abiding nowhere.
Section Five: Seeing According to Reality (divided into two parts). The physical forms of ordinary people all belong to the illusory and are not real; what is seen is not true seeing.

This principle of suchness alone is the original nature of humanity; it is the ultimate reality. It is not seen with the eyes, but seen with the mind; it is not sought through the perception of forms, but sought through the perception of principle. This is true seeing.
"Subhūti, what do you think? ... That which the Tathāgata has described as the marks of the body is precisely not the body.

[Note] This "Tathāgata" refers to the Buddha of True Nature (*dharmatā-buddha*). He is serene and eternally abiding; fundamentally without arising or ceasing, he is that which cannot be seen through marks.
"Body" refers to the form-body (*rūpa-kāya*); "marks" refers to the various characteristics. "Precisely not the marks of the body" means that it is not the form-body.
All these marks are not real.
[Commentary] The Buddha said to Subhūti: "I say that a bodhisattva who trains in the Way should abide as instructed and seek nothing else apart from this.
This is because a Tathāgata cannot be sought through physical traces. What is your opinion on this?
"How so? Can one see the Tathāgata by means of the marks of physical form? Subhūti, understanding his meaning, replied: "No, World-Honored One.
One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the marks of the body. Why is it that he cannot be seen by means of the marks of the body?
It is because the marks of the body spoken of by the Tathāgata do not exceed the mere physical form."
It is merely the end product of provisional combination. How could it be said that one sees the True Tathāgata by means of a body-form that exists as a reality?
Therefore, it is said: "it is precisely not a body-form."
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever marks there are... if one perceives all marks as no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
[Note] What are called "all marks" do not refer merely to physical characteristics; all phenomena, whether they are dharmic marks or non-dharmic marks, are included therein.
Yet, when the mind does not cling, one perceives that all marks are no-marks;
this is what the Tathāgata refers to as the Dharma-body. [Commentary] The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Since the Tathāgata cannot be sought through marks, you should see that whatever exists in the world with form and appearance is merely a provisional combination; it is not something inherently real. Although...

Having form and appearance is likewise but a delusion. If you can perceive all such signs as being manifestations that are not the true fundamental nature, you will naturally be free from the error of clinging to appearances and losing sight of the truth.
You will then be able to turn the light inward and reflect back, seeing the true nature of the Dharma-body, which manifests everywhere according to the Tathāgata.

Chapter Six: The Rarity of Right Faith (divided into two sections). In the study of the Way, faith is the foundation. Hearing the true teaching—that the Dharma of the Mahāyāna is without abiding and without marks—is rare indeed.
(Without doubt or fear, it constitutes right faith. Such a person is not easily found; therefore, it is rare.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [up to] ...one obtains such immeasurable merit."

[Note] "White" (bái) refers to a formal announcement. "Pho" (頗) means somewhat abbreviated. "Chapters" (zhāng) are divided; "sentences" (jù) are read. "True faith" (shíxìn) refers to genuine confidence.

Such spoken chapters and sentences refer to the words of the aforementioned [sections on] the three, four, and five divisions, as well as the teachings on non-abiding practice in giving and the signless vision of the Buddha.
Regarding the "latter five hundred years," the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states that there are five periods.
Five hundred years. In the first five hundred years, liberation will be firm; in the second, meditative concentration (dhyāna) will be firm;
in the third, learning (bahuśruta) will be firm; in the fourth, stūpas and monasteries will be firm; and in the fifth, contention will be firm.

When the sutras refer to "the latter five hundred years," they point to the period of the Final Dharma (mappō) characterized by contention. Even then, there will still be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit. Upholding...
Regarding "precepts": do no evil. Regarding "cultivating merit": practice all that is good. Regarding "roots": they possess the meaning of growth.
To give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment, to focus one's mindfulness exclusively, and to be free from defilement and attachment—this is called "pure faith."
This refers to both merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). That which is enjoyed in the world is the retribution of merit;
one who believes in this sutra is said to possess "merit" (*puṇya*), meaning they possess both merit and virtue (*guṇa*).

[Commentary: Subhūti had deep faith in what the Buddha had spoken. Fearing that those who would hear the Dharma in the future might not be able to believe and accept it, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All that the World-Honored One has taught is the authentic teaching of the Mahāyāna;
there are no Bodhisattvas who do not believe, accept, and practice it. However, among ordinary sentient beings, there are many who, upon hearing such [teachings]..."
One practices giving without dwelling [upon it]. As for the words and phrases concerning "true emptiness" and "signlessness," can one truly believe them?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not look down upon sentient beings by saying that they cannot produce such true faith.

It is simply because they do not dwell in the wondrous principle of true emptiness; this principle is inherently possessed by the human mind, yet it is obscured by the six sense objects and the four marks."
It is merely that they are obscured and thus remain in ignorance. There will surely be virtuous people of great capacity who can naturally trust in this Way.

Even after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, there will be virtuous people who observe the precepts and cultivate merit, who are able to place even a single chapter or a single phrase of this sutra within their hearts with faith. By means of this—
This is a true statement. You should know that this person’s roots of goodness have been cultivated most deeply;
it cannot be that they planted these roots under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas.
They have already performed every worldly deed that benefits things and aids people among the presence of immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas. And...
Having planted various roots of goodness and brought them to fruition, one attains this genuine faith; it is not something that can be attained by those of shallow faculties.

If there is a person possessing such roots of goodness who hears even a single phrase of this sutra, and for even a single moment of thought maintains purity without distraction, and believes without doubt—this pure and faithful mind is what the Tathāgata [praises].
As for those who do not possess this pure and faithful mind... [the Tathāgata] does not [grant them his full protection].
They can verify and know it; they can fully embrace and perceive it.
Although those who possess such faith are called sentient beings, the merit obtained through their pure faith is inexhaustible in its enjoyment—how could it possibly have any limit?
Why is this? Because these sentient beings no longer possess the mark of self (up to: even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas).
[Note] The first "why" states that pure faith and merit reside in the signless (*animitta*). The second "why" [states that...].
It is said that this is because they are without marks (*animitta*). Thirdly, as for why: the "simpleton" (the unenlightened person) says it is redundant.

This explains the reason for generating faith and attaining merit. It encompasses both the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); being without the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the emptiness of persons.
There is no mark of dharmas, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas; this is the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmasūnyatā*).

The marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span—indeed, all marks throughout the entirety of heaven and earth—do not transcend these. "Non-dharma" means the absence of dharmas; to "sink into" refers to falling into a state of dull emptiness (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*).
To "take" is to grasp. One who takes marks with the mind is not transformed within this [teaching]; failing to realize the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), they yet desire to grasp it.
One seeks by means of marks; this constitutes an external obstruction. Therefore, it is said that one is "attached to the four marks.

Although the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) do not compare to those of material form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*), if there is even the slightest grasping at them, one likewise fails to awaken to the essence of true emptiness and gives rise to an internal obstruction.

Thus, it is also said that one is "attached to what is not-dharma" (*adharmābhiniveśa*). Fundamentally, one does not depart from marks; how much less so when one clings to them? One who is attached to the four marks is precisely not [a Bodhisattva].
Because he is a bodhisattva, he must be without grasping and without attachment; only then does he accord with true emptiness. Therefore, one should not grasp at it;
thus, the Tathāgata has always employed the analogy of the raft.
【Lecture】 The Buddha said: "As for these sentient beings, for what reason do they obtain such merit?
It is because that single thought of generating pure faith is, in reality, the ripening of their roots of goodness; it is able to accord with the principle of true emptiness and signlessness.
They no longer possess the four marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span, nor do they have any attachment to the words and phrases of this sutra."

To fall into the view of existence and treat it as a characteristic of dharmas, or likewise to fail to contemplate and investigate their words, remaining submerged in emptiness and guarding silence, is to fall into the view of non-existence and treat it as a non-dharma characteristic.
One should not cling to either of the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
One restores the nature of true emptiness; all marks are completely relinquished, and the mind is free from defiled attachment.
This is why one has pure faith in this sutra and acquires immeasurable merit. The Buddha further spoke of it conversely: for what reason?
If these sentient beings were not empty in mind and grasped at formal characteristics, they would immediately be dragged into attachment to self, person, and sentient beings.
This concerns the traces of the "life-span possessor" (jīvaka). How could one possibly cause the nature and mind to be empty and luminous, responding to conditions as they arise?
This is what people find easy to understand. As for my statement that there are no marks of dharmas, it is because of the fundamentally empty true essence.
It does not reside within words or letters. If one grasps at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it is no different from the previous mind that clings to the four marks.
As for non-dharmas, they are without marks. I also say there is no such thing as a mark of non-dharma;
for within true nature (*bhūtatathatā*), all phenomena manifest without allowing even a hair’s breadth of defiled attachment. Originally, they do not [interfere with] one another.
Obstruction. If one grasps at the marks of non-dharmas, calling this "unrecorded," "emptiness," "annihilationism," or "nihilism," this mind will not be transformed.
How does this differ from the previous attachment to the four marks? Therefore, regarding both dharmas and non-dharmas, these two extremes of view must be severed.
One should not grasp at them as existent and thereby take up dharmas, nor should one grasp at them as nonexistent and thereby take up non-dharmas.
Regarding the Dharma, there is also a fundamental reason for this principle that it should not be grasped. The Tathāgata once said:
"You bhikṣus who study the Path should know that I have taught this Dharma because you possess four characteristics and are unable to realize true emptiness and transcend to the other shore.
Therefore, I provisionally employ this Dharma to enable you to cross over and be liberated from the ocean of suffering of birth and death."
Listen. Once you have realized your original mind and attained the bliss of nirvana, even the Dharma I have taught should no longer be relied upon.
It is like weaving bamboo into a raft to help people cross water; once they reach the shore, the raft is no longer needed.
If even the Dharma should be relinquished, how much more so should one not be attached to what is neither-dharma-nor-non-dharma? Furthermore, why should one grasp at it?

Section Seven: Neither Attainment nor Explanation The principle of unsurpassed Bodhi is originally without marks. Upon the emptiness of its very substance, there is nothing that can be attained and no words by which it can be explained.
"Subhūti, what do you think? ... [up to] ... all have their distinctions based on the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
[Note]: *Ye* is a term of doubt; it is also a term of interrogation. The bodhicitta is the original nature of the Tathāgata, and it is likewise possessed by all people.
How could it be something obtained from the outside alone, such that it must depend upon words to be manifested? As for 'definitively' (*ding*):"
To be mired in a single location is to lack penetration. It is not that phenomena (*dharma*) do not exist; it is not that non-phenomena (*adharma*) do not exist.
That which is neither existent nor non-existent is the ultimate principle. Therefore, the character "yi" (以) follows from what precedes; in all cases, the character "yi" is employed here.
The Dharma of Non-action (*wuwei fa*) is an alternative name for unsurpassed *bodhi*; it is spontaneous (*ziran*).

The nature of awakening (*bodhicitta*) does not depend on human artifice. Some say that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are mundane phenomena, while unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are supramundane phenomena.
In essence, however, it is through unconditioned phenomena that distinctions arise; thus, even the conditioned is fundamentally rooted in the unconditioned.
To differentiate between existence and non-existence is what is meant by "distinction. Most people in the world [view it] in this way...
Regarding the two characters "wuwei" (unconditioned): to take them to mean "making the heart like ash and the body like withered wood," such that one does nothing at all, is truly a foolish view.

Those who have attained the Way to a shallow degree are called "worthy ones" (xian); those who have attained the Way to a deep degree are called "sages" (sheng). To point to what is already manifest is to speak of their differing distinctions;

it is also to speak of their disparities and classifications. (Note: The character "cha" in "bielucha" has two pronunciations: one is *chā* [initial *chū yá*], and the other is *cí* [initial *chū yí*]).

According to the original commentary on the ancient manuscript, the character was originally read as *chà* (different). Later, there were those who read it as *cī* (uneven/discrepant). If explained in terms of the varying depths of the sages and saints, it should be read as *cī*. If explained in terms of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it should be read as *chà*.
However, since the sense of "unevenness" is inherent within "difference," both pronunciations may be correctly applied; one need not be strictly restricted to one.
[Commentary] Since the previous chapter stated that one should not grasp at dharmas and that they are like a raft, it was feared that Subhūti had not yet fully penetrated this point;
therefore, another question is posed: "What do you think? Regarding the unsurpassed bodhi-dharma of the Tathāgata..."
"If there is something sought, is it obtained within oneself? Or is it that by means of this Dharma one speaks of it and teaches it to others?

Subhūti replied, "According to how I have realized the meaning of what the Buddha has taught within my own mind, I know that even the Dharma of Unsurpassed, Perfect, and Complete Enlightenment is but a provisional designation.
If one seeks it, it is ultimately unobtainable; it is primordial."
There is no fixed, existent dharma; this is indeed the meaning of that name. It is as the Tathāgata has taught:
he merely establishes teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings in order to awaken them. Having no choice but to speak, he nonetheless speaks of no fixed, existent dharma.
There is no fixed name nor any fixed teaching upon which the Tathāgata can rely to speak. The reason why the Tathāgata’s Dharma has neither fixed names nor fixed explanations is as follows:
Why is this? It is because that which the Tathāgata has taught is the Dharma of unsurpassed bodhi.
It can be awakened to by the mind, but it cannot be grasped through signs; were there even a single thought of grasping, one would be distracted by seeking externally.

It can be transmitted by the mind, but it cannot be bestowed through words; were there even a single utterance, one would become mired in literary expressions. Neither of these is permissible. This is so.
It is the Dharma. If one clings to it as being the Dharma, subtle and unfathomable—existing yet not existing—where would the Dharma be? It is not the Dharma.
If one clings to it as being non-Dharma, responding immediately to conditions—non-existent yet not non-existing—how could it reside in non-Dharma?
Furthermore, it is not even "not non-Dharma. How then can it be designated by a fixed name or explained with fixed words? This is why it is so.
Why is this so? The Dharma is fundamentally rooted in non-existence (*wu*). It is precisely because it is non-existent that it is wondrous.
Although all these worthies and sages differ in their temporal sequence—whether earlier or later, distant or near—none can transcend non-existence as the basis of their Dharma.
There are merely differences in the depth of their realization and the adaptation of their function to specific capacities. Thus, they appear distinct from one another.
Chapter Eight: Arising in Accordance with the Dharma (The "Dharma" refers to the Dharma of this very sutra, specifically the Prajñāpāramitā. "In accordance with" means not to contradict it.
All the sublime Dharmas of the Buddhas arise entirely in reliance upon this Dharma).
"Subhūti, what do you think? (Up to: That which is called 'Buddha-dharma' is not, in fact, Buddha-dharma.
[Note: Regarding the "trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*): "world" (*loka*) refers to the flow of time, and "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial boundaries.
Past, future, and present constitute the "worlds" (*loka*). East, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below constitute the "realms" (*dhātu*). Three thousand...

"Trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*) is a collective term for one great world-system, used here to describe its vast extent. "Generosity" (*dāna*) refers to the wide distribution and relinquishing [of wealth].
Regarding the "seven treasures"—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, pearl, and crystal—the phrase "how much would it be?
(*kiṃ nu khalu*) is an interrogative expression used to emphasize the calculation of their great quantity. As for the "four-line verse" (*catuṣpādikā gāthā*), various interpretations exist.
Some refer to two verses within the sutra, while others refer to the four lines on the mark of non-self (*anātman*). One must understand that the Buddha merely spoke these verses;

he did not exclusively adhere to one particular *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Rather, these are the essentials of the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*), intended to encourage people to receive and uphold these four-line verses, which either reveal the true nature (*dharmatā*) or clarify the wondrous Dharma.
Furthermore, they are the core of the sutra itself. To cling to one part while discarding the rest...
This misses the intent of the sutra. From beginning to end, this sutra discusses in its entirety the wondrous principle of true emptiness and formlessness (*śūnyatā-nimitta*).
If one can realize this essential meaning, where would there not be the refined composition of the text within these single fascicles?

As for "gāthā," it refers to sentences formed by spoken words. Regarding the phrase "four-line gāthā" and the use of "even as far as" (*yāvat*) or "and so forth" (*ādi*), these indicate a range from many to few.

[Commentary: It is not the case that a verse is restricted to four lines; one must understand it by looking at the essential meaning, even down to individual characters such as "乃至" (nàizhì) and "等" (děng). The rest is detailed in the *Guǎlù* (Extensive Record). [Lecture:
Subhūti certainly understands the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), yet he does not know that one thereby attains immeasurable merit. The Buddha—
Desiring to reveal this merit of upholding the sutra to those in training, he first addressed Subhūti by name and said to him:
"Suppose there were someone who filled the three-thousandfold world system with the seven treasures and gave them as a gift;
would the merit obtained by that person be great or not? Subhūti, grasping the meaning, replied:
If a person were to practice giving with the seven treasures, their wealth would be abundant and their merit superior; the resulting virtue would indeed be vast.
This is truly as the World-Honored One has said. Why is this? Such merit arises from a giving characterized by signs (*nimitta*);

it is entirely unrelated to the principle of the true emptiness and signlessness within the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). It is by no means the natural merit inherent within that nature. Therefore...
The Tathāgata speaks of the great amount of merit merely because it is a provisional aggregation; thus, its abundance is perceived. The Buddha said:

"If there is a person who, regarding the words within this sutra, directly accepts them without forgetting, reverently upholds them without weariness, and even by distilling the broad into the concise, explains four-line verses and the like for others—"
This principle constitutes both self-benefit and the benefit of others. It is not merely awakening to the nature of oneself alone, but awakening to the nature of all people as well.
One shall see that the merit obtained from the simultaneous fulfillment of both self and others far exceeds that of the aforementioned gift of the seven treasures.
Yet, why is it superior to that? For it is because the *prajñā* of true emptiness is...
The principle of the marks is the fundamental nature of all Buddhas. The multitude of all Buddhas and the dharma of the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas all flow forth from this sutra.
In seeking a direct pointing to the whole body [of reality], there has never been anything as clear and exhaustive as this sutra.
Furthermore, the Buddha feared that people would become mired in the Buddha-dharma; thus, he again called out, "Subhūti..."
Bodhi enlightened him, saying: "That which is called the Buddha-dharma fundamentally does not exist.
It is merely a provisional means to awaken sentient beings, enabling them to see their own nature in an instant; thus it is named 'Buddha-dharma.
Therefore it is said, 'It is precisely not the Buddha-dharma,' for this serves to sweep away all attachments and reveal the true emptiness of Prajñā."

Chapter Nine: On the Single Characteristic and the Absence of Characteristics (The "single characteristic" refers to the fact that each of the four fruits of practice possesses its own characteristic. Although their actual cultivation follows a sequential order, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is one.)

Although the fruits differ in depth, one must in no way harbor a mind that seeks to acquire them. One should instead cultivate profound realization to enter the signless (animitta). For even the stages such as Srotāpanna are merely provisional names; ultimately, from the very beginning, there is not even a single characteristic.
"Subhūti, what do you think? [up to] "...and thus he is named Subhūti, who delights in the practice of araṇā.
[Note: The Sanskrit term for *srotāpanna* is *srotāpanna*; this is translated here as "entering the stream," meaning entering the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*).
"There is nothing entered" means not being attached to the characteristics of entering the stream. The word "I" refers to those such as the *srotāpanna*. The Sanskrit term is *srotāpanna*.
Sakṛdāgāmin. This is translated as "One Who Returns Once. It means that when a deluded thought arises in the preceding moment, the succeeding moment immediately ceases it;
when the preceding moment has attachment, the succeeding moment immediately detaches from it. Deluded thoughts come and go within the mind:
when they go, the deluded thoughts cease, yet they may still return once more because the fundamental nature has not yet attained quiescence. The Sanskrit term is Anāgāmin, which is translated as...
He does not come back; he does not return to the desire realm. This is also called "transcending desire. Externally there are no objects of desire, and internally there is no mind of desire;
this means that the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-kleśa*) have already been severed. In Sanskrit, he is called *arhat*; here it is translated as "one who has left desire.

His mind has already realized the essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted. He possesses no fruit of birth and death of his own, just as a tree that has finished bearing fruit.
This means that one who has reached the path of this stage attains the principle of signlessness; it is not merely a fruit.
Furthermore, as for the fruit of Srotāpanna (Stream-enterer), afflictions do not arise, and one is determined never to enter the hells or other realms of rebirth;
this is called the first fruit, like the initial sprouting of a fruit. As for the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner), the physical body returns only once more.
Coming to the heavens or the human realm is like fruit that is still large and unripe. As for the fruit of *anāgāmin* (non-returner), the habitual tendencies of desire are forever exhausted;
they are certain not to come back to receive birth in the desire realm, like fruit that is about to ripen.

As for the *arhat*, both mind and environment are empty, and inner and outer are eternally tranquil. Since phenomena are truly non-existent, how could one form the thought of having attained the Way? It is like...

This refers to those whose fruit has already ripened. In the Sanskrit language it is *samādhi*; here it is translated as "Right Concentration" (*zhèngdìng*) and also as "Right Awakening" (*zhèngjué*).
It is the sensation of bliss. In the Sanskrit language it is *araṇa*; here it is translated as "Non-contention" (*wúzhēng*). When it sprouts in the mind, it is called "recollection" (*niàn*);

when it manifests in action, it is called "conduct" (*xíng*). This means that because one lacks the view of self and others (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), one does not give rise to contentious conduct. In truth, there is nothing to be practiced.
The fundamental nature is empty and quiescent; it responds to conditions and accords with stimuli, yet in reality, there is no mind that performs any action.
[Commentary] The Buddha asked Subhūti: "Does a Srotāpanna harbor the thought, 'I shall certainly attain this fruit'?
Subhūti knew this was not so, and thus said: "A Srotāpanna does not give rise to the notion of attaining the fruit."
What is the nature of this mind? It is because he has already transcended ordinary perceptions and his mind inclines toward the principle of formlessness (*animitta*).

He attains a state akin to that of the sages, yet there is nothing into which he enters. Regarding the thought of the realm of the sages, he merely restrains his desires and does not enter the spheres of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
Is it not in this that the Srotāpanna derives his name? Thus spoke the Buddha.
He asked again: "Does a Sakṛdāgāmin harbor a thought, thinking to himself, 'I shall certainly attain this fruit'?
Subhūti replied that this was not so, saying: "The mind of a Sakṛdāgāmin has already reached the stage of ultimate stillness;
however, when encountering various objects, he is unable to remain unmoved by them. There is still one more cycle of birth and death, yet there is no further [rebirth]."
Second is arising and ceasing: as soon as the preceding thought becomes attached, the succeeding thought immediately awakens to it. One does not dwell long upon human desires;
although one may come and go between the human realm and the heavens, this is called "one coming and going," yet in reality there is no coming or going.
Is this perhaps the origin of the name *Sakṛdāgāmin*? The Buddha asked again: "When an *Anāgāmin* forms a thought, they say to themselves, 'I...'"
"Will one necessarily attain this fruit? Subhūti replied, "Not so. One who is an Anāgāmin has an empty mind regarding desire.
Having already severed the delusions of thought within the realm of dust, they do not perceive external objects as desirable.

Because they do not return to take birth in the Desire Realm, they are called 'Non-returners' (Anāgāmin). Now, to say 'non-returning' implies that this mind has not yet been fully dissolved; it still..."
There is the labor of forced exertion, yet in reality there are no traces of anything not coming forth.

This is because not only are the six sense organs pure and tranquil, but one also perceives that the six objects of perception are fundamentally empty. This has already reached an excellent state—could this not be what is meant by an Anāgāmin?
The Buddha asked again: "An Arhat forms a thought, saying to himself, 'I have attained this...'"
Someone said, "Is it not so? Subhūti knew this was not the case, and he replied: "Arhatship is also a provisional name.
The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally empty; in reality, there is no dharma that can be called 'Arhat.

If an Arhat were to harbor the thought that they have attained the Way, the mind of attainment would still not be eliminated, and they would immediately become attached to the four [perversions], such as the self and persons."
"It is so. How could I be worthy of the title 'Arhat'? Subhūti further brought forth what he had personally realized from the Buddha’s teachings and testified to it, saying:
'World-Honored One, the Buddha once said in the past: "I, Subhūti, have not given rise to a single thought;
all dharmas are without contention. Having attained this samādhi, among all the disciples, I am permitted to be the foremost."'"
"I must certainly have exhausted all human passions; only then will you grant that I am an Arhat free from desire.
Although the World-Honored One granted that I was an Arhat free from desire, I did not entertain the thought, "I am an Arhat free from desire.
Furthermore, fearing that the great assembly might not know that I had abandoned the mind of attainment, I called upon the World-Honored One to speak in detail.
He said: "If I were to harbor such a thought as 'I must certainly attain the path of Arhatship,' then another delusive conception would arise.

How then could the six realms of desire be suddenly emptied? It was for this reason that the World-Honored One did not, among his great disciples, declare me, Subhūti, to be one who delights in tranquility or one who possesses such conduct free from contention. Thus it was because of Subhūti...
Although Subhūti appears to have outward conduct, within he truly has no mind that engages in such conduct;
only then can I say that Subhūti delights in the practice of araṇā.

Section Ten: Adorning the Pure Land (divided into three parts). “Adornment” (*vyūha*) means magnificent decoration. “Pure Land” (*śuddhakṣetra*) refers to a pure world, that is, the Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*).

This section speaks of the purification of the mind-ground within the objective realm, thereby accomplishing adornment. If the mind-ground is not pure, one returns to the [ordinary] Buddha-fields. Within their own nature, the Bodhisattvas are profoundly serene and pure; with no attachments or entanglements in the mind, they naturally possess an adorned realm.

This section speaks of the Buddha-field from the perspective of the mind, for it is established by the mind. Thus, the Bodhisattvas attend to the mind below while attending to the land; they accomplish adornment such that the land is naturally nothing but pure. Only when these three meanings are combined is the whole complete.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "What do you think? [up to] "...in reality, there is nothing to be attained regarding dharmas.
[Note]: "Tathāgata" is what the Buddha refers to himself; it means "one who has come thus. Dīpaṃkara Buddha is the same as Dīpaṅkara Buddha.

When that Buddha was born, the light from his body was like a lamp, hence he was named Dīpaṃkara (Lamp-Maker). He was the teacher who bestowed the prophecy upon Śākyamuni Buddha. There is... [text continues].
"Attainment. This refers to the dharma of having something to be attained.

[Commentary] The Buddha [observed that] although the various bodhisattvas had heard the teaching that all four fruits are ultimately unattainable, their sense of attainment had not yet been eliminated.
They still harbored doubts, thinking that the Buddha-dharma was not entirely non-existent, and clung to the notion that there were dharmas in which one could abide. Therefore, he addressed Subhūti:

Pṛṣṭha said: "What do you think? When I was originally with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, having heard and received the Dharma and attained the fruit of the unsurpassed path, did I obtain the Dharma of my original teacher? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One. Although the Tathāgata heard the Dharma from his original teacher, it was nothing other than his own awakening."

Through cultivation and guided by a teacher, one achieves unsurpassed bodhi. In reality, however, there has never been any dharma that could be considered a secret transmission or a lineage handed down from a teacher.
"Subhūti, what do you think? [up to] "one should generate the mind without dwelling on anything. [Note]:

Adornment (*vyūha*) is spoken of in terms of the objective realm (*viṣaya*). "Adorn" (*zhuāng*) means upright decoration; "adorn" (*yán*) means orderly and meticulous refinement. When spoken of in terms of the mind:

that the true nature (*tathatā*) is not disturbed is called "adorned" (*zhuāng*); that false delusions do not enter is called "adorned" (*yán*). Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*): this is spoken of in terms of the objective realm.
This refers to the Buddha-world. When one speaks of "mind," it points to the original ground of mind;

what is called the "Buddha-land" means that the Buddha-mind does not lose its original nature and is thus able to perfect the ground of mind. This is analogous to how the Confucianists speak of the Way, which ultimately resides in the sage.
Among the five elements, earth resides in the center and gives birth to all things. The mind abides in the central path and gives birth to all dharmas;

therefore, earth is used as a metaphor for the mind. Furthermore, because there must be one Buddha who establishes his transformation within every world, a world is also called a "Buddha-field" (*buddhakṣetra*).
"Is not" (*fei*) is a term for negation and elimination; "is named" (*shi ming*) is a sense of provisional establishment. Or it is said:
This is not a non-dual understanding; it is called "having two meanings. The first is that this name exists only as a provisional designation (*prajñapti*).

The second is that it is precisely by means of this [designation] that there is naming. One should understand these according to the text. Shengxian said: "That which is 'not' is the 'name'"; the meanings correspond to one another.
This grammatical method is used extensively throughout the sutras; in all cases, it serves the function of negating provisional establishments in order to reveal the ultimate meaning.
"Is not" means that it exists from the void; this is called "single function. "Is named" refers to why it has traditionally been called the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

Taking the destruction of appearances to reveal the truth as its central tenet, and the elimination of the provisional to establish the ultimate as its correct principle—this is how one interprets the scripture.

There are those who take "is precisely not" (*jìfēi*) as pointing to the true mark (*shíxiàng*). For example, regarding "precisely not the marks of the body": they claim that what is "not the marks of the body" is the true mark.
This involves breaking the connection at the character "is" (*jí*) and joining the character "not" (*fēi*) with the following phrase to create a sense of indirect indication (*zhuǎnzhǐ*).

This is called "making it into 'is precisely'. There are also very many who provide such an interpretation within their exegesis of the sutra; this "is precisely not" is also [interpreted in this way].

There are two meanings. To carefully examine the text of the sutra, it is appropriate to regard this as a process of elimination and clearing away; it is certainly not a refutation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Refuting characteristics is precisely intended to reveal the ultimate reality (*tattva*). The subtlety lies in its lack of explicit verbalization. As the former masters said: "It causes people to realize and understand it for themselves."
To interpret this as "turning the finger" is to overreach one's intent; while the explanation may seem subtle, it actually obscures the meaning of the scripture.

It is like pointing directly at something and breaking it open—just as chewing wax yields nothing. The repeated interrogations in the subsequent passages would all become unnecessary [under such an interpretation].
One must know that form is itself formlessness; only upon reaching the section on the "principle of the single identity" does one finally clarify what has preceded.
All of these are merely dismissals; they have never been explicitly refuted. The term "bodhisattvas" refers to practitioners.
The title "Mahāsattva" (Great Being) is indeed appropriate. The two characters "thus" (*evam*) refer to what is stated in the following text:
"one who dwells nowhere," meaning one who does not abide with attachment in any single place, nor remain stuck and untransformed.
[The Teacher] said: The Buddha asked Subhūti, "Since there is ultimately nothing to be attained regarding the Dharma, what do you think?
When I consider the place where a Bodhisattva dwells, I call it a 'Buddha-field.

Does a Bodhisattva, within that Buddha-field, truly have the intention to perform virtuous causes and meritorious deeds, necessarily seeking to adorn themselves with the marks and signs [of a Buddha]? Subhūti deeply understood.
The Buddha’s intention was to answer according to principle, saying: "As for the claim that a bodhisattva adorns a buddha-field, such a statement is not correct, World-Honored One.
Why is this? For a bodhisattva’s adornment of a buddha-field does not consist in external appearances or physical traces.
If one were to consider only things such as palaces of the seven treasures or buildings with five-colored rafters as constituting adornment—"
Adorning the Buddha-land: that which is adorned through illusion is unreal; it is not truly adornment, for it is merely a false name called "adornment.

How could a bodhisattva intentionally adorn a Buddha-land? Because Subhūti was able to grasp the Buddha’s intent, the Buddha spoke to him in accordance with his words: "Therefore, Subhūti, since the adornment of a bodhisattva..."
If one focuses on external adornments, one must seek within the mind. Now, the mind is fundamentally pure; it becomes impure when enticed by sensory objects and transformed by them.
Once one realizes that in the Buddha-dharma there is nothing to be attained, and further realizes that adornment is not true adornment, this is the pure mind free from grasping and attachment.
All bodhisattvas training in the Way should act accordingly.
This is profound stillness, eternally empty and unstained; it is tranquil stillness, eternally settled and undisturbed. By means of this, one gives rise to a pure mind.
One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling upon forms and colors, nor should one give rise to the mind by dwelling upon sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects (*dharmas*).
To have any point of dwelling is to be bound by the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); thus, deluded thoughts will arise in succession. Do not...
One is thus able to attain purity. One must know that the pure mind is wondrously perfect and all-pervasive; it does not adhere to specific locations, for it fundamentally has no place of abiding.
One should generate the mind within this state of non-abiding. Like a bright mirror placed before one, it reflects everything as objects approach and becomes empty again as they depart.
Naturally, the ground of the mind becomes pure, unrestricted by location. This is the true [mind].
It is an adornment. If the adornments of a Buddha-field or a world-system are all merely conventional fruits, conventional designations, and illusory appearances, how can they be worth calculating?
Subhūti, it is as if there were a person... [as far as] the Buddha says that what is not a body is called a "great body."

[Note] Regarding the King of Mountains, Sumeru: because this mountain stands at the center of the four continents and is the greatest of all mountains, it is called the "King of Mountains" (Shanwang), meaning it reigns as the sovereign among all peaks.
It is three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand *li* in height and breadth; the sun and moon revolve around this mountain, thereby creating day and night.
It is divided into four parts, forming the four continents, with the Heaven of the Thirty-three above them;

this may be called exceedingly vast. Using this as a metaphor for the size of the human body is merely a figurative expression, similar to descriptions such as the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm.
[Commentary] The Buddha called to Subhūti and said to him: "Suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains.
What do you think? Could it be considered large? Subhūti, having deeply realized the Buddha’s intent, replied:
"A body as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains, is indeed large. However, how could such a large body [possess...]"
This is what is meant by "great. If one speaks in terms of a body of physical form, how could there be such greatness?
That which the Buddha has taught is not a body of physical form; it is precisely this that is called the "Great Body."

Chapter Eleven: The Superiority of the Merit of the Unconditioned (The unconditioned dharmas; "superior merit" refers to cultivation. The merit of these unconditioned dharmas surpasses that of giving the seven treasures of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

For the merit of upholding this sutra benefits both oneself and others; it does not depend on deliberate effort. Compared to the merit of other conditioned acts of giving, this merit of the unconditioned is far more superior.)
"Subhūti, as many grains of sand as there are in the Ganges River... [omitted] ...this merit surpasses the former merit. [Note]:
There is a river in the Western Regions called the Gaṅgā. It flows eastward from Lake Anavatapta and encircles forty *li*.
The Buddha frequently preached the Dharma here; therefore, it was taken as a metaphor. This was because it was something familiar to his disciples' experience, so that they might understand.
This is easy to understand. The phrase "sand of the Ganges" is an inverted construction, meaning that the Ganges is as numerous as its sands.
[Commentary] The Buddha first poses a question using things easily perceived by all people: "Subhūti, regarding the number of things in the world..."
There is none that does not have its measure of more or less. The number of all the sands in the Ganges River is difficult to measure.
Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand—what do you think? Would the number of grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers be great?
Subhūti replied, "It would be very much so. He then addressed the World-Honored One again:
He said: "Even the Ganges rivers, which are like grains of sand and so forth, are already numerous and their number is inexhaustible;
how much more so the sands within those rivers—how could their number ever be exhausted? The Buddha said to Subhūti:
'I now tell you with words of truth: if there were good men or good women who, with the most precious of the seven treasures,' "
"Suppose there were objects filling as many three-thousandfold world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and one were to give them as a gift to others.
Would the fruit of merit obtained from this be great? Subhūti replied that it would indeed be very much so.
He then addressed the World-Honored One to confirm his meaning, saying: "If such giving results in merit, how could there be..."
"It is not that the principle is not clear; it is simply that I do not know what the Blessed One thinks of it. The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If you were to give gifts of the seven treasures, would the merit thereby obtained be great? "It would indeed be great," he replied.
"If there were a son or daughter of good family who, from this sutra, were to take even as little as a four-line verse and, with faith, receive it into their heart and realize its meaning..."
As for "meaning" (*yi*): to firmly uphold it in the mind and preserve its principle is to internally perceive true nature;
thus, one is no longer deluded by karmic consciousness and is further able to explain it to others so that they may hear and receive it, enabling them likewise to believe without doubt.
Maintaining this without loss, the mind-ground becomes clear and bright, and there arises a gradual awakening to the true nature. After a long time, one's roots of goodness will all ripen;
one can then escape saṃsāra and achieve the unsurpassed path. Thus, both self and others are benefited, and such merit is indeed the merit of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Compared to the merit received by those who practice the giving of the seven treasures, this is truly far more superior.

Chapter Twelve: Honoring the True Teaching (The True Teaching is the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Taking this as one's teaching constitutes the True Teaching. The Buddha established his teaching through the dharma of Bodhi;

it consists entirely of principles for exhausting one’s nature and reaching the ultimate of life, a discourse that is upright, great, and free from error. If a person can honor and revere it, clarifying the mind and seeing the nature to realize the true emptiness, they are upholding the True Teaching. Both devas and humans will give rise to reverence).
Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is preached—up to the point where there are those who respect it as if there were a Buddha or his honored disciples—[wherever this is said]:

"Wherever" means that, regardless of sequence, with a mind free from discrimination, wherever one may be, and without distinguishing between ordinary people and sages, one preaches this sutra by guiding and transforming others according to their capacities whenever one encounters them. One should know that "this place" refers to...

Regarding the place where this sutra was preached: "Devas" refers to the celestial realm, such as the class of the Four Heavenly Kings and others. "Humans" refers to the human realm, namely the people of the world.
"Asuras" refers to the realm of the Asura deities; this is translated as "Non-Heavenly Beings. Because their karmic retribution is most excellent, they rank immediately next to the various heavens;
although they enjoy heavenly blessings in proximity to them, they follow the path of non-heavenly beings. (The Asuras have [births from] the womb, egg, moisture, and...)

There are four types of transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) are able to sustain the world-system; they possess power and fearlessness, and contend for authority with Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings. This class has the gravest nature of anger (*dveṣa*), yet they are capable of protecting the Buddha’s Dharma.

Those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*) belong to the human realm (*manuṣyagati*); those born from an egg (*aṇḍaja*) belong to the realm of hungry ghosts (*pretagati*); and those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*) belong to the realm of animals (*tiryaggati*). Generally speaking, it is because their anger and resentment are so heavy that they take birth in the divine path (*devayoni*), though their karmic retributions differ.
Among the six paths of existence, the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals are not mentioned here because these three are characterized by the delusion of the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
