[Note: The 'form-body' refers to the thirty-two marks. 'All marks' means the various manifestations of supernatural powers;
furthermore, they do not stop at the thirty-two marks. 'Endowed' means there is no lack whatsoever. Form..."
The Lord of the Body speaks of being detached from form; the Lords of the Marks speak of being detached from marks. [Commentary:
Previously it was said that the body and its marks are not marks, and that all marks are non-marks. Subhūti already knew that there is a Dharma-body and Dharma-marks.
This follows upon the previous statement that the merit of the unconditioned is greater than the merit of conditioned things. The Buddha feared that Subhūti, because of suchness—
Regarding the coming of the form-body (rūpakāya), he regarded it as the dharma-body (dharmakāya). He then posed a question, saying: "Can the Buddha be seen by means of his perfected form-body?
Subhūti immediately understood his intention and replied: "No, World-Honored One. The nature of awakening is empty space."
It is not confined by form; one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of a perfected physical body (*rūpakāya*). Why is this?
That which the Tathāgata calls a "perfected physical body" is but a manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*) created by illusion; it is not a truly existent perfected physical body.
It is merely designated as a "perfected physical body. How, then, could one perceive the Tathāgata by means of a physical body?
The Buddha again asked Subhūti: "Can the Tathāgata’s manifested marks of supernatural power—his possession of all marks—be seen by means of those very marks?
Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One. For all marks are merely physical forms;
although they are complete, one should not perceive the Tathāgata through them. Why is this?"
That which the Tathāgata has spoken regarding the "perfection of all marks" refers merely to the external manifestations of physical forms;
it does not mean that there truly exists such perfection of marks. This is what is called the "perfection of all marks. How could one perceive the Tathāgata by means of these marks?
Section Twenty-One: On That Which Is Not Spoken and That Which Is Spoken (divided into two parts). Unsurpassed Bodhi is the primordial true nature; it cannot be expressed by words.

Yet, for the sake of awakening sentient beings, the Tathāgata employs speech as a means of transformation and guidance to expound Prajñāpāramitā. One must understand that the Dharma being taught is precisely for the sake of this which cannot be expressed by words—that is, it is spoken as something ineffable.
Subhūti, do not say that the Tathāgata has such a thought (up to: "there is no dharma that can be taught; this is called teaching the Dharma").
[Note] "Do not say" (*mò*)—*mò* and *zuò* (do) are both prohibitive terms. This means: do not say that within the Tathāgata’s mind he thinks to himself...
"I shall preach the Dharma to deliver the multitudes. This is because the Tathāgata awakens beings according to their respective faculties and capacities;

from the very beginning, he has never possessed a mind that intends to preach the Dharma. To say that there is something preached as Dharma is to fail to understand the essential purpose of preaching the Dharma;
it contradicts the Buddha’s intent—how could this be anything other than slander? For the original nature is empty and true. There is...
How can it be spoken? What is now called "preaching the Dharma" is merely a name; there is no actual dharma that can be spoken.
[Commentary] The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not think that the Tathāgata has a mind that gives rise to this thought:
'I shall preach some dharma to reveal and instruct others. You must absolutely not harbor such a notion. Why is this?"
Therefore, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has preached any Dharma, such a person possesses shallow views and meager knowledge;
they remain mired in the trivialities of words and phrases, contradicting the wondrous truth of true emptiness, and thus slander the Buddha, being unable to understand or realize it.
This is because of the meaning of what I have taught. Furthermore, he addressed Subhūti, saying:

"You should know that what is called 'preaching the Dharma,' although manifested through words, is nevertheless communicated through awakening. It is the silent realization of the source of the mind, which cannot be reached by speech.
There is no dharma that can be preached; this is what is called preaching the Dharma. Indeed, to preach while there is nothing to be preached is what is meant by preaching the Dharma."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] “that which is not a sentient being is called a ‘sentient being.
[Note: “At that time” refers to the moment of initiating the inquiry. “Wisdom-life” (*āyuṣmat*) is so called because he possesses wisdom as his virtue;

“life” (*āyuṣ*) is so called because of his longevity. This refers to one who possesses wisdom and is of advanced age and seniority. When a person reaches old age and decrepitude, they become dull-witted and senile.
[Such instances] are many. Subhūti attained the eye of wisdom despite his old age; being advanced in years yet possessed of virtue, his reputation moved the multitude.
[Commentary: At that time, Subhūti, who possessed wisdom and had penetrated the source of life, was profoundly in accord with the Buddha’s intent.

Fearing that what is "the teaching of non-teaching" could only be known by those endowed with the Buddha's wisdom—and that sentient beings might not necessarily know it—he [refrained from speaking]. Furthermore, if they do not know...

"How could one believe it? He then addressed the Buddha, saying, "Is there perhaps any sentient being in future ages who, upon hearing the Dharma that cannot be spoken as taught by the Tathāgata, can give rise to genuine faith and have no doubts?
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "Do not worry that in future ages there will be no sentient beings who believe in the Buddha-dharma."
Birth. Indeed, Buddhas and sentient beings are not originally two distinct categories; they both equally possess this mind.
While he is a sentient being, his true nature has existed from the beginning and cannot be defined merely by the term "sentient being.

Although he is not [merely] a sentient being, his karmic conditions are manifest in the present, and thus he cannot be defined as anything other than a sentient being. Why is this? Because sentient beings, amidst the multitude...

Among those born, those who cannot transcend and be liberated do so because they fail to repent and awaken; they renew their self-indulgence and self-abandonment, and thus become what we call "sentient beings.
If it is as the Tathāgata has taught—that human nature is universally good—then what distinction is there between the ordinary person and the sage?
Originally, there are no truly existent sentient beings; they are merely designated by the provisional name "sentient beings. Their fundamental nature is sovereign and at ease.
Having heard what the Buddha has spoken, how could one not give rise to faith?
○ Chapter Twenty-Two: No Dharma Can Be Attained (Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is originally true emptiness; since even the self does not exist, how much less so any dharma? Therefore it is said:
"No dharma can be attained.")
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[Commentary: Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "Our Buddha has exhausted all delusion and perfected enlightenment, attaining this Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Is it not because all dharmas are universally empty, perfectly luminous, quiescent, and illuminating, such that no further effort is required?"
To seek externally is precisely to have nothing attained; is this not, then, true attainment?
The Buddha deeply concurred with Subhūti’s question and affirmed it again, saying: "So it is, so it is. Regarding my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I did not attain it from without;
it is my own true nature. This true nature is like empty space, wherein spirit is concentrated and wisdom is clarified."
All things are extinguished; emotions are severed and thought is clarified. It cannot be grasped through physical forms, nor can it be sought through verbal expression.
There is not the slightest dharma that can be attained. This state of cessation is established only to guide sentient beings;
therefore, it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It serves merely to let people know where to take refuge—how could there be any dharma to be attained?

Section Twenty-Three: Purifying the Mind and Practicing Goodness (The wondrous nature is empty and quiescent; fundamentally, no dharma can be obtained. Yet, if one wishes to attain unsurpassed bodhi, what must be cultivated?

One must necessarily purify the mind and practice all manner of wholesome deeds. Taking this method as the gateway for entering the Way. Zongle says: "Purifying the mind and practicing goodness" means to perform these wholesome dharmas with a mind that does not cling to a single dharma).
Furthermore, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal (up to: it is not a wholesome dharma; it is called a wholesome dharma. [Note:
This "Dharma" refers to the essence of bodhi-awakening. A dharma that is no-dharma is the true Dharma. "Equal" means that all who possess cognition must share the same essence.
There is no distinction of high or low; it is not that the noble ones possess it while the ordinary do not.
It is deficient. Because it does not increase in the Sage, it is said to have no height; because it does not decrease in the ordinary person, it is said to have no lowness.
All wholesome dharmas—such as generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and so forth—are like this.
[Commentary] Ānanda further compiled and arranged [the teachings]. The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "This Dharma of Bodhi is ineffable and unattainable;
it is the primordial nature, fundamentally equal from the beginning. It does not diminish among sentient beings, nor does it increase among the Buddhas.
There is neither sage nor ordinary person. While the physical body has its high and low, the true nature is from the outset without [distinction]."
The distinction between high and low is precisely what is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is it so named?
Because within the true nature (*dharmatā*), there are no delusions regarding the four marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span;
it is because one perceives only equality that this name exists. The dharma of equality does not arise from a [fixed] nature.
Externally, one may attain [realization]. However, does this mean that cultivation and verification are to be abandoned?

If one were to claim that the original state is already perfected and thus requires no further practice, this would be to abandon the Dharma and sink into emptiness—a state of delusion from which one does not return.

Only by relying on a mind of equality and formlessness, cultivating all the wholesome dharmas of the six perfections and ten thousand practices, can one empty the self to contain the truth; from this, clarity arises.
When the mind perceives its own nature and reaches the stage of supreme awakening, one immediately attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is what is meant by self-cultivation and self-realization: that truly not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
Subhūti, it is not only that there is no dharma to be grasped in *bodhi*; even all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), which ought to be cultivated, likewise cannot be [grasped].
To cling [to them] is a mistake. What is called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*) is nothing more than a means to guide sentient beings and awaken the deluded masses.
Once awakening to Bodhi, what "wholesome dharmas" could there be? Originally, within one's own nature, these dharmas do not exist at all.

The Tathāgata said that what is called "wholesome dharmas" is precisely not wholesome dharmas; it is merely designated as "wholesome dharmas. These dharmas are not substantially existent, and thus they cannot be clung to.
It is indeed like mud! That there is not even the slightest dharma to be attained within Bodhi becomes even more clearly evident.

Section Twenty-Four: On the Incomparable Merit and Wisdom (*puṇyajñāna-asamabhāga*). (Merit refers to *puṇya*; wisdom refers to *jñāna*. When one practices with attachment to signs, it serves as the cause for rebirth among gods and humans as a state of outflow;

this can only be called "merit. To uphold this sutra and expound its teachings constitutes the immeasurable function of one’s original nature; thus, one possesses not only merit but also wisdom. This union of merit and wisdom is equal to empty space, beyond all comparison.)
Subhūti, if [the quantity of] the seven treasures in a trichiliocosm... [up to] ...cannot be reached by calculation or analogy. [Note]:
Such accumulations of the seven treasures refer to the vast amount gathered; they are equated with the height and greatness of Sumeru, the King of Mountains.
The Buddha, by virtue of the merit within his nature, is the most supreme; he is for the sake of the world.
Because people falsely cling to causes and conditions and seek the abundance of karmic rewards, [the Buddha] teaches according to their capacities, repeating the instruction over and over.
This is to shatter people’s attachment to the marks of conditioned, false merit, and to urge them instead to cultivate the body and the nature. [Commentary:
The preceding section stated that all wholesome dharmas are empty; fearing that people might again regard the scriptural text as mere empty talk, [the author] speaks of merit...
By comparing their virtues, one is led to know how to cultivate oneself. The Buddha told Subhūti: "Sumeru is the king of all mountains;
it may be called high and great. Yet, compared to all the mountains within the trichiliocosm..."
If one were to pile up the seven treasures as high and vast as Mount Sumeru, and were to give them away in such a manner, the merit resulting from that generosity would indeed be great and abundant.

Yet, if one is deluded regarding one's own nature (*svabhāva*), the merit of giving will eventually be exhausted, and one cannot avoid falling [into lower realms]. What can merit save in such a case? Of what benefit is it to one's nature? Suppose...

If there is anyone who, by means of this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, or even as little as a four-line verse, upholds it so that it enters their heart, recites it, and explains its meaning, they will not merely deliver themselves, but will also be able to deliver others;
their benefit will be inexhaustible. This is the cultivation of the merit and wisdom of one's own nature, which surpasses the giving of these seven treasures.
The merit of that [other] virtue does not equal even one hundredth part of the merit of upholding this sutra. How could it stop at one hundredth part?
Even a thousand million billionth part, or as many as can be calculated by number, or as vast as any analogy, cannot equal even this one part.
Can a person seek only the merit of giving while failing to cultivate the merit of their own nature?

Chapter Twenty-Five: Transformation and the Absence of Those to Be Transformed "Transformation" refers to the deliverance of sentient beings. "The absence of those to be transformed" means that, in reality, there are no sentient beings who attain *nirvāṇa*.

Although the Buddha establishes the Dharma to transform the multitudes, this Dharma is not established by force. Sentient beings inherently possess Buddha-nature; they have never originally been ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). It is merely that he guides them according to their own original nature. Thus, while there is "transformation," it ultimately results in the "absence of those to be transformed."
"Subhūti, what do you think? [From here until: 'He is not an ordinary person; he is called an ordinary person. [Note:

Those who have not yet crossed over are called sentient beings (*sattva*). After they have crossed over, they are no longer sentient beings. Being no longer sentient beings, they are devoid of the mark of a sentient being."
Therefore it is said: "In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers. When the Tathāgata speaks of a self, he does so only in reference to ordinary people.
The physical body is fundamentally empty; where, then, is a self? It is only because ordinary people do not realize this.
[The deluded] falsely identify with the physical body, taking it to be the self. [Commentary:
When the Tathāgata saves sentient beings, he manifests boundless bodies and preaches immeasurable Dharmas; this is the actual practice of his realization.
Each and every one is perfectly complete; it is not something a bodhisattva can attain. How could one say that there is no nirvana?
One simply does not realize that this Dharma is equal, and thus sentient beings are from the beginning quiescent and extinguished.
The Tathāgata merely establishes the Dharma to deliver them because they are sentient beings. The Tathāgata does not harbor the thought of delivering beings; therefore, he is able to deliver them.
Therefore, he called out to Subhūti and said to him: "What do you think?
You who study the Way, let no one among you say that the Tathāgata truly has this thought: 'I shall employ the Dharma to transform and deliver sentient beings.'"
You should not entertain such thoughts. Why is this? It is because the true nature of *prajñā* is fully possessed by every person.
Although the Tathāgata delivers them through the Dharma, he merely delivers that which is already present; there is nothing therein to be added.
That which is fundamentally non-existent returns to non-existence; in truth, there are no sentient beings who are delivered by the Tathāgata. Suppose, however, that...
To see sentient beings as those to be delivered by the Tathāgata is for the Tathāgata to perceive that "I" am able to deliver and transform them;

this constitutes the existence of a self (*ātman*). Because of my delivering them, there is the existence of a person (*pudgala*). Delivering people so they leave behind the dust of defilement and ascend to my Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
There are sentient beings who cross over from birth and death and do not enter saṃsāra;
there are those with a life-span who do not forget for even a single thought-moment, yet they possess all four marks. This is what is called the "Equal True Dharma Realm.
As for the statement that "the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings," how could the Tathāgata possibly have such a thing? Since the Tathāgata is devoid of the four marks, how could he have a self?
However, when the Tathāgata speaks of a "self," he does so in reference to sentient beings; it is not that there is a truly existent self.

Yet ordinary people mistakenly grasp at illusory appearances and believe there is a self, for they have not yet seen their true nature (dharmatā), and thus the notion of a self-identity has not been forgotten.
Furthermore, fearing that others might discriminate between the Buddha and ordinary beings, the Buddha again addressed Subhūti.
He said: "Ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) appear to differ from the Tathāgata; yet, if one discusses their fundamental nature, it is empty tranquility and sovereign freedom.
If one can truly awaken to this, one enters into Bodhi accordingly. Therefore, the Tathāgata says that they are not ordinary beings at all—they are merely designated as 'ordinary beings' by name.
Thus, the Tathāgata and ordinary beings are one and the same. Furthermore, how could there be a Tathāgata who is able to deliver them?"
Come! You are indeed beings who may be delivered. Section Twenty-Six:
The Dharma-body is Without Characteristics. (The Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body emerges from the fundamental nature; it is thus true emptiness and does not belong to the realm of appearances.)

There is no mark to be sought; it must first be realized through the mind before it can be attained. It cannot be seen through physical forms, for all such forms belong to the realm of illusion, and whatever is perceived therein is not real. Thus it is said: "The Dharmakāya has no marks."
"Subhūti, what do you think? [Up to: One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. [Note:

A Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) is the legitimate sovereign of the four heavens who governs the four great continents. In the first, fifth, and ninth months, he illuminates Jambudvīpa in the south;
in the second, sixth, and tenth months, he illuminates Aparagoyānī in the west; in the third, seventh, and eleventh...
The moon shines upon Uttarakuru in the north; for four, eight, twelve, or sixteen months, it shines upon Pūrvavideha in the east, revolving constantly like a wheel.

It observes the good and evil among human beings to govern the four continents. This is the second bhūmi bodhisattva, who dwells provisionally in the rank of a Golden Wheel-turning King to practice his cultivation.
Although he remains within the realms of gods and humans, he has not yet transcended the three realms, owing to the blessings resulting from his karmic retribution.
Virtue. He is likewise endowed with the thirty-two marks; these are accomplished through the power of karma. "Contemplation" (*guan*) and "seeing" (*jian*) are not the same.
"Seeing" refers to the essence of contemplation itself. "Contemplation" refers to the act of contemplating in this manner—contemplating by means of the mind.
[Commentary: Since the preceding section stated that the Tathāgata is without self, and being without self implies being without marks, the Buddha feared that sentient beings...
Because the view that clings to marks had not yet been eliminated, he asked Subhūti again:
"The Tathāgata’s appearance is dignified and majestic, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks. What do you think? Can the Tathāgata truly be perceived by means of these thirty-two marks?
Subhūti, following the Buddha’s words, replied accordingly: "So it is, so it is. Indeed...
To recognize [the Tathāgata] by means of observing his marks is what Subhūti is being questioned about. The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of marks;
yet he can be observed through marks. Because there are these marks, it is not that one cannot observe the subtlety of the markless (animitta). It is never impossible.
This answer given by Subhūti is not incorrect; it is precisely the point where he has attained profound understanding and made progress.

However, it does not accord with the Buddha’s intent in posing the question. When beginners hear this, they will fail to realize that it is through the signless (*animitta*) that one can manifest signs.
They will merely perceive signs and remain ignorant of the signless, inevitably clinging to signs to contemplate the Tathāgata, thereby falling into error.
Because it is a false path, the Buddha questioned him back to enlighten him, saying:

"If the Tathāgata could be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), who governs the four continents and wanders throughout them without ceasing, would also possess the thirty-two marks due to his manifold meritorious deeds, and thus would be similar to the Tathāgata. This Wheel-Turning Sage King would then [be the Tathāgata]."
"You shall become a Tathāgata. Subhūti, having deeply realized the Buddha’s intention, immediately replied:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse: "Those who follow this person walk upon a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
[Note: A *gāthā* (verse) refers to speech formed into lines; furthermore, four lines constitute one verse. "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to color;

"to see" (*darśana*) means to behold with one's own eyes. "Sound" (*śabda*) refers to the tone of speech; "to seek" (*paryeṣaṇa*) refers to the resonance of the voice. "I" (*aham*) is the Buddha’s self-reference; here it points to the Dharma.
The self that is truly, eternally, and purely pure is also the "self" as it pertains to persons. Regarding those of heterodox paths: sound and form are merely illusory and false;
only the true nature (*dharmatā*) constitutes right awakening. The Tathāgata refers to this true nature as the *dharmakāya*.
[Commentary] At that time, the World-Honored One, having certified and elucidated the meaning, spoke in verse, saying: "The self of the Tathāgata..."

Fundamentally, there is no form that can be seen and no sound that can be sought. If a person seeks through form and pursues through sound, their mind wanders outside of the true nature and they fall into the realm of consciousness.
The conduct of such a person is called entering a false path; they will certainly be unable to see the Tathāgata.
This is because by seeking the Self within sound and form, they regard the Tathāgata as possessing marks. If one wishes to see the Tathāgata...
How could he be characterized by the thirty-two marks? [End of Section One. Part Two:

Neither Ceasing Nor Extinction. (The preceding section stated that he cannot be seen through form nor sought through sound; fearing that people might suspect that the Tathāgata has severed or extinguished all dharmas.)

To eliminate the appearance of form while failing to know the wondrous essence of true emptiness is due to the absence of the characteristic of annihilation; this section further elucidates this point. That is to say, because one takes all dharmas—which are inherently indestructible—as a basis for giving rise to the view of non-existence.
Subhūti, if you should have such a thought, it concerns the fact that regarding dharmas, I do not speak of their characteristic of annihilation. [Note:

"The characteristic of fulfillment" refers to what was previously called "being endowed with all characteristics. To speak of the annihilation of all dharmas means that "annihilation" (斷) is non-continuation and "extinction" (滅) is non-arising.
The wondrous nature is fundamentally empty, like a bright mirror unobscured by even the slightest speck of dust; it remains as it is.

The myriad forms arise and perish of their own accord, yet the luminous essence of the mirror remains in a state of tranquil illumination, suchness (*tathatā*), never undergoing interruption or cessation.
If one were to conceive the thought that the mirror was originally clouded by its own obscurations, then its light would be subject to obstruction and the characteristic of cessation.
This is because I say that those who seek *bodhi* must not harbor attachments even to "non-existence"; it is not that the Tathāgata [is non-existent].
It is not incorrect to say that one does not attain bodhi by means of the marks of perfection.
[Commentary] Continuing from the preceding text: Subhūti, although you know that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of his marks...
If you should entertain such a thought as this— namely, that the Tathāgata did not attain this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by virtue of possessing the marks of physical perfection,
but must have abandoned those marks and produced a different understanding— you must by no means harbor such a notion,
thinking that the Tathāgata is formless and without sound or color, and thus does not possess them.
It is because of the perfection of the marks of the feet that one attains this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind.

The Buddha further addressed him, saying: "If you were to entertain the thought that all marks are non-existent, as soon as you give rise to this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind, it would be said that all the dharmas for delivering sentient beings are completely severed."

"It has ceased. Although the Tathāgata is liberated from worldly conditions, perfectly penetrating and signless, and his spiritual transformations are without fixed direction, he nevertheless accords with and responds to conditions;

he is fundamentally not one who undergoes annihilation. If the Dharma were subject to annihilation, by what means could the nature of the mind manifest, and True Suchness would also nearly be extinguished.
You must by no means harbor such a thought. Why is this so? For all..."
Those who resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* must necessarily rely upon all phenomena as the path of their practice;
they cannot preach the Dharma while simultaneously discarding them or asserting the mark of annihilation.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: On Non-Receiving and Non-Attachment The merit and virtue produced by a Bodhisattva are all the true emptiness of Prajñā; they directly transcend to the other shore.

How can these be compared to the merit and virtue of worldly giving, which involves receiving and becoming attached? As for "non-receiving," it means being unstained by even a single speck of dust; even if there were [objects], where could they be attached? As for "non-attachment," it means the mind is equal to empty space; from where could desire and craving arise?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva [were to fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges]... for this reason it is said that they do not accept merit.
[Note: "I" refers to the mind of self-centeredness. "Accomplishment" (cheng) means to achieve or fulfill.
Previously, within the context of the six pāramitās, the pāramitā of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) was singled out for discussion; one can thus see how great the significance of patience is. People...
Regarding all matters, one clings to a single "self-mind," which gives rise to the four marks.
Upon the six sense objects, seeing what is lovely, one accepts it; seeing what is desirable, one craves it; and thus one becomes unable to endure [the contrary].

By thus subduing the mind, one remains far from Bodhi. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, there is the patience of acceptance (*anupatana-kṣānti*) and the patience of observation (*vipaśyanā-kṣānti*).
By cultivating these two types of patience, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In this context, the character "knowing" (*zhī*) refers to the patience of observation, and the character "accomplishing" (*chéng*) refers to the patience of acceptance; through knowing that all dharmas are without self, one achieves [this state].
Regarding patience, this is precisely the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena).

[Commentary: Since the preceding section already stated that one does not cling to the marks of sound or form, nor to the mark of annihilation, one has truly attained penetration into the dharma of non-self.
Therefore, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "Suppose a bodhisattva were to take [a world-system] as full as the Ganges..."
If one were to take the seven treasures of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them in charity, it could indeed be called much and the resulting merit would be supreme;
yet, this does not avoid the mind of greedy attachment, and thus it is not a merit of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, if there is another person...
He deeply understands that all phenomena arise from the mind; they are as profound and vast as empty space, neither abiding nor clinging, entirely equal, and devoid of the mark of self.
Although he universally delivers others through the gift of Dharma, he does not claim the ability to achieve it for himself.
By thus perfecting the thought of forbearance, this Bodhisattva’s merit of non-self surpasses the former.
This is the merit obtained by a Bodhisattva through the precious gift of Dharma. Yet, the reason why this excels [other merits] is: for what reason?

Because the minds of all Bodhisattvas are fundamentally without self (*anātman*). Since there is already the merit of the gift of Dharma, yet they lack the mind that thinks "I am giving," who is there to receive it?
It is precisely because they do not accept this merit that it is without limit; therefore, it surpasses the previous [merits].
This is the merit obtained by the Bodhisattva. Subhūti, not yet understanding the meaning of "not receiving," addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva thus obtains merit, he ought to receive and enjoy it. Why, then, does a bodhisattva not receive merit?
The Buddha answered Subhūti: "The merit from the giving performed by a bodhisattva is, in its essence, identical to the ultimate reality."
The nature of dharmas is selflessness; there is no mark of a self, nor is there a grasping mind.
From the beginning, [the Bodhisattva] acts for the benefit of sentient beings, not for his own personal enjoyment. If even a single thought of grasping for enjoyment arises, it becomes attachment.
When a Bodhisattva cultivates merit, he should not give rise to a mind of attachment. For this reason, it is said that he does not "accept" merit.
Chapter Twenty-nine: On the Tranquility of Dignified Manner (Īryāpatha-śānti). (The Tathāgata’s walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are called the four dignified manners (*īryāpatha*).

"Tranquility" means that within these dignified manners, the true nature is tranquil—neither going nor coming, suchness itself, unmoving. (This section points out tranquility from within the dignified manners; it reveals that the nature is unstained and free from arising and ceasing. One must not mistake the mere performance of dignified manners for tranquility itself.)
Subhūti, if someone were to say [up to] "he is called the Tathāgata because he has nowhere to go," [the commentary states]:
This section contains three instances where "Tathāgata" is mentioned; all refer to true nature (*dharmatā*). True nature is without marks (*animitta*).
If one attempts to describe it through the four modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*), that person does not understand the meaning and principle of the Tathāgata as taught by the Buddha. Therefore...
That which is called "Tathāgata" means there is neither going nor coming; this is the true meaning of "Tathāgata.
It is for this reason that he is named Tathāgata.
[Commentary: The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata pervades the void and the Dharma-realm; it is without marks and without location.
Whenever it manifests in response, it comes according to the karmic conditions of sentient beings. Yet its true nature remains as it is, never having left any trace of coming or going.
When people behold the majestic deportment of the Tathāgata’s responsive transformations, they realize that he is neither annihilated nor fallen into emptiness. Furthermore—
"It is not by falling into the perception of physical form that one can perceive the Tathāgata.

This is still to remain within conceptualization regarding the *nirmāṇakāya* (the body of response), and thus fail to penetrate thoroughly into the *dharmakāya* (the body of reality). Therefore, he addressed Subhūti, saying:
'If there were someone who said, "The Tathāgata comes"—meaning he responds through sympathetic resonance—or "he goes"—meaning he enters into quiescence.'"
Whether sitting in the full lotus posture or reclining at rest, it is by virtue of these four modes of deportment that one is designated as a Tathāgata.
This, however, is to be attached to signs; it is merely to behold his physical form without having glimpsed his true nature.
Such a person cannot understand my meaning of "Tathāgata. Why is this so? For one who understands it... [the reason follows].
That which is called the Tathāgata does not take manifested transformation as its essence, but takes the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as its essence.
It is the single suchness that pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*, eternally unmoving. Primordially devoid of coming or going, it abides because it shares the same essence as sentient beings.

Having given rise to compassionate vows to deliver all beings, throughout immeasurable eons it has universally cultivated all practices, perfuming them into pure karma. In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, it responds...
"Manifesting as salvation" means that when sentient beings' minds are pure, [the Buddha] appears as soon as the conditions arise; yet in coming, there is no place from which he comes.
"Departing" means that when sentient beings' minds are defiled, [the Buddha] vanishes once the response is completed; yet in departing, there is no place to which he goes.

Thus one knows that the true essence of the Dharmakāya is utterly devoid of coming and going; it is for this reason alone that he is called the Tathāgata. If he manifests and displays the four majestic postures...

These are merely traces manifested for the purpose of transforming and delivering sentient beings. Although these traces may involve movement or stillness, their essential nature is truly without movement or stillness.
How could one grasp at these traces and speak of them as the Tathāgata? Indeed, he comes from nowhere.
Thus it is not existent, yet there is nowhere to which it goes; thus it is not non-existent.

When the views of existence and non-existence are completely shattered, at this point, the doubts regarding the cessation of all phenomena—such as the perception of form and the seeking of sound—are thoroughly and fundamentally resolved.

Section Thirty: On the Principle of the Unified Whole (Zongle says: The Southern Tang stone edition and the New Prefecture Sixth Patriarch’s commentary both read “The Section on the Principle of the Unified Whole.

The Tathāgata’s possession of form is the *xiang* (phenomenon); the true nature’s being neither coming nor going is the *li* (principle). Without principle, phenomena have nothing to be subsumed; without phenomena, principle has nothing to which it may attach.
Only when the principle of true emptiness and the externally possessed phenomena merge into one are the interior and exterior fully integrated, such that the refined and the coarse are non-dual).
Subhūti, if good sons or good daughters (up to) even ordinary worldlings are greedily attached to those things. [Note:
The worlds of atoms do not exist as substantial realities at all; they are entirely provisional designations.

Therefore, within the worlds, the subtle vapors drift and waft, arising and ceasing according to their own course. Within the great void of space, there are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
Let them gather and disperse as they will; they are like the afflictions and the defiled mind within a human being, all of which arise by following after delusion.
Within every person’s body, there exists discursive thought; these subtle and miscellaneous notions are like the fine dust of the world.
Yet they are not things inherent within one's original nature, being nothing more than shadows, echoes, and empty illusions. Therefore it is said: "It is not this; it is merely a name."

Furthermore, as for the "single integrated mark" (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*), it is like Zhu Xi’s statement that "the vital energy (*qi*) forms the physical shape, while the principle (*li*) is also imparted to it.
"Single" means it cannot be divided into two; "integrated" means it cannot be analyzed into separation.

This refers to the integration of principle and form into a single mark. This is according to the Tathāgata’s words regarding the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the response body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
There is the Dharma-body. Based on the common person’s assertion that within the body of the four great elements there exists a true nature, one may extend this reasoning:
from the vastness of heaven and earth down to the smallest of all things, wherever there is form, there is likewise principle; yet principle cannot be manifested without form.

It is impossible for a form to manifest without [the conditions of] irrationality; all are but a single composite phenomenon (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*). When the Sūtra speaks of a "single composite phenomenon," it refers specifically to the human body.
The "dust-motes of the world" were previously cited as a metaphor. The provisional aggregation of the dust-body is no different from the provisional aggregation of the dust-world.
The dust-world constitutes the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*), while the dust-body constitutes the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*). This is because—

The receptacle world is followed by the enumeration of the world of sentient beings; therefore, the discourse proceeds from the minute particles of the world up to the "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*).
This is the same principle as what the Confucian texts state: "The human body is a small cosmos. What the Tathāgata says is so because the Buddha has previously spoken of it.
To say "it is not" means that it lacks substantial reality. To say "it is called by this name" means that it is a mere conventional designation.

Furthermore, within the karmic conditions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the Tathāgata manifests through responsive transformation according to conditions; this is called the "unified appearance" (*ekapiṇḍalaksana*). All of these are not real.
That which is real and without appearance cannot be described. It cannot be described because true nature (*bhūtatathatā*) is without appearance and thus ineffable.
Appearance is itself non-appearance; yet ordinary beings do not realize this and instead greedily cling to appearances.
Phenomenal appearances are, in truth, signless; they are the traces manifested by the true nature.

Ordinary beings, however, harbor craving and cling to them, just as the eyes see forms and become attached to forms, or the ears hear sounds and become attached to sounds. They become mired in this physical body and mistakenly identify it as the self;
thus, they sink into the six realms of existence with no means of liberation. This is precisely what makes them ordinary beings.

[Commentary] The preceding passage stated that there is nowhere from which it comes and nowhere to which it goes; thus, one should know that the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is entirely the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

It does not fall into the single view of existence or non-existence. However, I fear that people will give rise to interpretations based on the literal words, perceiving the dharma-body as dispersing into a response-body at the point where there is coming and going, and thereby claiming that the Tathāgata dwells in a separate location. As for the [point] where there is no coming...

There is no place of departure. When one sees that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is subsumed within and returns to the *dharmakāya* (dharma body), one might then claim that the Tathāgata dwells in a single location or dwells in various locations.
To see all phenomena as truly existing, or for phenomena not to return to suchness (*tathatā*), is to see the characteristics of things as incapable of vanishing.
To dwell in a single location is to hold that the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) cannot be signless; yet, [this is contrary to] Bodhi.

There is a Dharma which wisdom illuminates without extinguishing it. That Tathāgata, within the Dharma-realm, manifests transformations according to conditions, flowing together with them without obstruction;
he does not abide in one place, nor does he abide in a different place.

Therefore, by citing the unreality of the atoms of the world, he uses this as a metaphor for how the Dharmakāya’s manifestations are neither identical nor different, yet concludes by returning to the mark of the unified whole.

To clarify this, the Buddha said to Subhūti: "If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who were to take a trichiliocosm and grind it into a mass of fine dust, what do you think?
Would that multitude of fine dust particles be numerous? Subhūti, having realized the meaning, replied: "If one were to divide a world into fine dust particles..."
"Very many, World-Honored One. What is the meaning of that which you have said? If these aggregates of atoms were truly existent as a multitude of fruits, everyone would know it;
why would it be necessary for the Buddha to speak of it? The Buddha does not say that these are a multitude of atoms. Why, then, did he speak of them?
He broke down the elements into dust, showing that these delusive dusts are a phantom-like aggregation. Thus do worldly people [perceive].
This is not understood; therefore, it must be explained by the Buddha. That which the Buddha calls a "multitude of atoms" is not a truly existent multitude of atoms;
it is merely a false designation called a "multitude of atoms. Subhūti then addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Not only are atoms unreal, but even the trichiliocosm spoken of by the Tathāgata is entirely an illusion formed by the accumulation of dust."
It is formed. Yet when the kalpas reach their end, it too undergoes transformation and decay. For this reason, it is empty and not substantial;
it is not a world in the true sense, but because it is empty, it is called a "world. Why is this?

If one were to regard the world as substantially existent, then since a world is formed by the aggregation of many atoms, it would constitute a "unified whole" (*ekaghanasamjñā*) that could be grasped as real.
"There is indeed such a thing. That which the Tathāgata calls a 'unified whole' (ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa) is formed through the illusory combination of the four great elements and the five aggregates;
it is a concretion of principle and qi, a provisional union of essence and appearance. There is no truly existing unified whole; it is merely a conventional designation called a 'unified whole.
When the Buddha heard Subhūti’s words, knowing that he had profoundly realized this principle, he called out to him and said:"
He said: "This so-called 'single unified mark' is real yet not real; it is a mark yet not a mark. Thus, it cannot be sought through verbal expression;
the true nature resides therein. However, ordinary people, upon hearing the Buddhas' teachings, are unable to realize them.
At the shallow level, they greedily cling to the various sensory objects, causing conditions to arise in competition; at the deep level, they greedily cling to form."
As they attend to these marks, illusory appearances increase ever further; they consequently become bound by the discursive thoughts of arising and ceasing and are unable to attain liberation.
How could they know that the union of principle and appearance is the ineffable wonder?

Chapter Thirty-one: On the Non-arising of Knowledge and Views The original nature is fundamentally empty, true, and pure. It is unconditioned true knowledge that illuminates everything without exception.

As soon as one gives rise to conceptual knowledge and views, whatever is perceived is nothing other than the four marks [of existence], making it difficult to give rise to the unsurpassed mind of Bodhi. Only when these deluded knowledges and views are completely extinguished and do not arise can the perception of the four marks naturally cease, and the true knowledge of Prajñā be revealed.

Thus one may realize Bodhi and ascend to the other shore. [Shengxian said: "The true nature is fundamentally such that views do not arise. These words clarify the true nature; one must understand that this means views do not arise.]

Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Buddha taught "the view of self" (ātma-dṛṣṭi)—up to "it is not the characteristic of dharmas, but is called the characteristic of dharmas"—[this refers to the following].
[Note: Previously, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) were mentioned; here, the four views (*dṛṣṭi*) are mentioned. A "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which is manifested by a dharma;

a "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is that which is grasped by the mind. However, while the characteristic is coarse, the view is subtle. The "four views" refers to the views that construct the four characteristics. (Third repetition)
To speak of this: it is the Buddha’s analysis of the meaning of discarding the view of the body to realize the nature.

If a person lacks knowledge and vision, they are the same as a block of dull stone; how could the Buddha lack them? It is simply that there are true and false forms of knowledge and vision. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

"Hearing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, manifesting the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is the truth of knowledge and vision.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "To establish a knowing within seeing is the very root of ignorance;
this is the delusion of that seeing. Wang Rixiu said: "Seeing" means to regard seeing as truly existent.

Once one is fixated on reality, one becomes attached to many things, and deluded thoughts flourish. "Dharma" refers to the principle of phenomena; "marks" (xiàng) refers to external traces and appearances.

Regarding the non-arising of the marks of dharmas: concerning the traces of phenomenal dharmas, such views as those of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span do not sprout within the mind at all.
To know and see in this way is the true knowledge and true vision of unsurpassed bodhi.
This is not merely the elimination of names and marks to exhaust them; it is called [the realization of the Dharma-body].
The manifestation of dharmic characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is the exhaustion of the true nature (*tattvalakṣaṇa*). [Commentary:
Previously, one merely destroyed characteristics; here, one destroys views. If the mind of views is not destroyed, the boundaries of identity and difference will not be eliminated.

Therefore, he combines and refutes [these views]. It is because the Buddha feared that people would cling to false views, which would obstruct true vision and prevent them from realizing the true nature.

Thus, he called out to Subhūti and asked: "If someone were to say that what the Buddha has taught truly contains the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span—Subhūti, what do you think?"
"What do you think? Would such a person be able to understand the meaning of what I have taught? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One.
Although such a person may be able to speak the words, their mind cannot realize them; they cannot understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught.
Why is it that they cannot understand? Because, World-Honored One, regarding what the Buddha has taught concerning 'self' and 'person'..."

The views of sentient beings as having a life-span or a self are originally external manifestations and false appearances; they are not the true reality within the nature, nor do these views actually exist.

Because sentient beings are obstructed by the private attachments of form and trace, and flow into the burdensome transformations of material things, these four views are provisionally established as names to sweep away their clinging to signs for the sake of sentient beings; thus they are called "self" and "person."
Sentient beings and a life-span are like this; how could such views truly exist?
Because of Subhūti’s words regarding the three repetitions and four views, the Buddha analyzed them with clarity. He then called him by name and told him:
"In general, for one who has resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, not only are the four marks appropriate to be empty, but even at the level of a single..."
All dharmas are entirely without marks (*animitta*). One should recognize one’s own fundamental mind and perceive one’s own original nature;
there ought to be such true knowledge, such true vision, and such faith, acceptance, understanding, and realization that not even a hair’s breadth of dharma-marks arises.
As for "dharma-marks," they refer to the various dharmas practiced in cultivation; if one becomes attached to even a single one, then all marks will arise.
Non-arising is supreme enlightenment; it is a state of total, natural spontaneity. As for external forms and traces, none of them should be regarded as a burden.
However, for a beginner, if they do not rely on the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there will be no means by which they may enter.
Subhūti, all that I have spoken regarding the characteristics of dharmas is merely for the purpose of guiding beginners and causing them to progress gradually.

If one reaches the ultimate penetration of the true nature, which is empty and quiescent, how could there be any characteristics of dharmas? Therefore, the Tathāgata said that they are not truly existent characteristics of dharmas;

they are merely provisional designations of dharma-characteristics. Now, since the characteristics of dharmas do not exist, there must necessarily be no views of self, person, sentient being, or life-span.
It is here that the true nature of Prajñā can be realized, and the Bodhicitta is awakened.
The mind should examine this with care. Section Thirty-Two:

The Manifestations of Response Are Not Real (divided into three parts). This section clarifies that while ordinary beings manifest appearances and establish transformations externally through phenomena, these are ultimately not real.

Only the self-so-ness of the fundamental nature is real. Throughout this entire chapter of the sutra, the teaching is repeated again and again, all converging upon the fact that true emptiness and formlessness are the self-nature itself. It is fundamentally empty space; do not grasp at forms. Suchness.

The two phrases "immovable" exhaustively encompass this. To be unmoving in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*) is precisely true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The entire sūtra was expounded for the sake of delivering sentient beings; therefore, it concludes with "expounding. Deliverance returns to non-deliverance, and exposition returns to non-exposition—this is not the ultimate truth.
Subhūti, if there were someone who, with [a world-system] filled to its utmost extent, up to and including immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, did not grasp at signs and remained unmoving in suchness.
[Note: *Asaṃkhyeya* is a numerical designation in the Western lands (India); it is simply called "the infinite.
An immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* represents the ultimate limit of accumulated numbers; it cannot be calculated by ordinary reckoning. One who has resolved upon the bodhicitta is said to...
This refers to generating the vast aspiration to deliver and save all sentient beings. To deduce and clarify the meaning of the sutras is called "expounding" (*yan*);
to proclaim and disseminate the meaning of the sutras is called "explaining" (*shuo*). Regarding "as-it-is immovable": the upper character *ru* (如) refers to the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*);
the lower character *ru* refers to being exceedingly as-it-is. "Immovable" means not shifting or moving in pursuit of appearances.

[Commentary]: The general meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā* has already been explained above. Now, the Tathāgata wishes for future generations to uphold and expound this sutra so as to transmit the life of wisdom (*prajñājīva*).
For this reason, he again calls upon Subhūti and addresses him, saying:
"If there were someone who, with the seven treasures filling immeasurable and incalculable worlds, were to take them and give them as alms, the merit they would obtain could indeed be called great."
However, one cannot abandon the characteristics of giving material wealth; though such merit is great, it will ultimately come to an end.
As for the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, it is entirely the wondrous truth of the Dharmakāya. All Buddhas and the dharma of unsurpassed Bodhi all emerge from this.
I only fear that people will regard it merely as written words and fail to uphold it with their hearts.
They delight in maintaining a narrow-minded resolve, rather than maintaining the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva.

If there are good men or good women who give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment to deliver all beings and faithfully uphold it with sincerity, their merit from upholding even a single four-line verse from within this sutra is not merely rare;
it is truly extraordinary. It is not in vain that they uphold even such a portion of this sutra.
One clarifies one's own nature for oneself and further expounds it for others, teaching them likewise to clarify their own nature.
Thus, both self and others are perfected, and the benefit is inexhaustible. The merit thereby obtained surpasses that of one who gives the seven treasures in charity.
The Buddha spoke again, saying: "Regarding what I call 'expounding the Dharma for others,' do you know how to expound it for others?
It is simply not to grasp at appearances, remaining as suchness and unmoving. For both myself and sentient beings, we are all but a provisional combination of form and characteristics.
If one speaks of true nature, it does not cling to the four marks and does not dwell within the six sense objects; thus, both person and phenomena are transcended."
Forgetfulness: when both emotion and intellect are extinguished, there are naturally no traces to be sought, nor are there any sounds or forms to be seen. It is primordial emptiness;
how could there be any characteristics to be grasped? There is only the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), which manifests in response to all things without anything being contrary to its intent.
It is simply suchness. Its spiritual powers pervade the dharma-realm, yet its concentration is spontaneous;
it performs wondrous transformations without fixed direction, yet its essence is eternally quiescent. Pervading the realm of empty space, it abides forever in sovereign freedom.
From the beginning, how could it ever have followed the shifting of appearances to undergo any movement within? This is truly that which can be expounded.
Why is this? All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—up to [the point where it says] "like dew and like lightning"—should be viewed in this manner.
[Note: "Phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to the phenomena of things. "Conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) means that which is produced through volitional activity.

From the transformative cultivation of heaven and earth above, down to the human activities of creation and action below, all are conditioned phenomena. "Dream" refers to dreaming while asleep. Sleep...

At that time, although there appears to be cognition, it is entirely non-existent. "Illusion" (*māyā*) refers to magical arts, such as tying a cloth into the shape of a rabbit or binding grass into the form of a horse;
all such things are empty illusions and lack reality. "Bubbles" refers to water bubbles; though they possess external appearances, they are actually void within.
"Reflections" refers to reflected forms; they exist when light strikes them and vanish when the light ceases. "Dew" refers to morning dew.
If damp in the morning, it remains; if dried by the sun during the day, it becomes dry. "Electricity" refers to lightning, which appears suddenly and vanishes as quickly as the blinking of an eyelid.
These two characters refer to the aforementioned six things.
【Lecture】 The Buddha further explained of his own accord: "That which I speak of as not grasping at marks and being unmoving as such—why is this so?
It is because the fundamental nature is empty and without marks; it is originally suchness (*tathatā*), devoid of any deliberate activity.
Therefore, all ordinary beings, sages, and worthies take non-action (*wuwei*) as their Dharma and personally realize it. If there were anything..."
[All things] are created; they are thus merely empty, false, and unreal. Therefore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world are like dreams and not real;
like illusions produced by sorcery; like bubbles on water, floating and hollow;
like shadows, flickering and indistinct; like morning dew, easily dried up; like lightning, easily extinguished. One should regard them as such.
These six are the observations. One may observe that the affairs of the world are characterized by the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
they arise and perish, and are not truly real. Only the nature of suchness (*tathatā*), which is immovable, is as profound and vast as empty space;
it exists eternally beyond ten thousand kalpas and remains unchanging through a thousand transformations. To expound upon its merits—how could they ever be measured?
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Elder Subhūti [and the rest] were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
[Note: This section consists of Ānanda’s record of the words; it is the standard conclusion of a sutra, known as the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) section.
"Propagation" means the propagation of Prajñāpāramitā to benefit sentient beings, like water that is not obstructed.
"Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs" refers to the two assemblies of men and women who have left the household life.
"Upāsakas and upāsikās" refers to the two assemblies of men and women who remain in the household life. "Devas, humans, and asuras" refers to three of the six realms of existence.

This is the Way. Although the beginning of the sutra merely mentions "the great assembly of bhikṣus," the present mention of the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings clarifies that those previously mentioned were not absent from the gathering when the sutra was first preached.
Whatever one hears with joy will surely be wondrously harmonized with the mind.
If one accords with this, one will believe it; if one receives it with true earnestness, one will practice it without fail.
[Commentary] Because the Buddha had repeatedly elucidated the Dharma of Prajñā, Ānanda recorded it and said:
"When my Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, the Elder who was the first to request instruction, named Subhūti, suddenly—"
He realized the true emptiness and silently received the seal of the mind.
At that time, among those present who heard the Dharma were bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās, as well as all people of the world, devas from the heavens, and asura spirits.
Having heard this sutra spoken by the Buddha, each person attained realization at the moment his words fell upon them.
By nature, they were neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid; instead, they all gave rise to great joy at having encountered the True Dharma.
There was none who did not believe and accept his words, holding them in their hearts, practicing his teachings, and expounding them to others.
Although he has spent billions of kalpas to eternally realize Bodhi, he has simultaneously delivered both himself and others.
This is precisely the compassion of our Buddha, who extensively constructs ferries and bridges to deliver the masses of the deluded; his merit for this world is truly beyond measure.
